Based on Vahe Movsisyan’s AUA lectures 3 and 4. Learn the method, follow the arithmetic, then connect it to R.

Binary Dependent Variables

Model the probability of a yes/no outcome, rather than treating 0 and 1 as an ordinary continuous response.

Lecture 3, slides 1–5

Why a binary outcome needs its own model

A binary variable records one of two outcomes. Code the event you want to predict as 1 and its complement as 0. The lecture examples include attending college, driving to work, buying rather than renting a house, and deciding to advertise. In the bank example, 1 means accepting a personal loan. The numerical code is a label: an observed customer cannot have an outcome of 0.36, but many comparable customers can have a 36% chance of acceptance.

Ordinary linear regression models a numerical response with an additive error. If applied directly to a 0/1 response, its fitted line can fall below 0 or above 1. Its errors are also not normally distributed and its conditional variance changes with the probability. Logistic regression solves the range problem by modeling log-odds and converting the answer back to a probability.

Bernoulli response

Yi∣xi∼Bernoulli⁡(pi),P(Yi=yi)=piyi(1−pi)1−yiY_i\mid\mathbf x_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),\quad P(Y_i=y_i)=p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}Yi​∣xi​∼Bernoulli(pi​),P(Yi​=yi​)=piyi​​(1−pi​)1−yi​

Here i labels a customer; Yᵢ is their random 0/1 outcome; yᵢ is its observed value; xᵢ is their predictor information; pᵢ is P(Yᵢ=1 | xᵢ). The expression applies only for yᵢ=0 or 1.

pi=0.36:P(Yi=1)=0.36,P(Yi=0)=0.64p_i=0.36:\quad P(Y_i=1)=0.36,\quad P(Y_i=0)=0.64pi​=0.36:P(Yi​=1)=0.36,P(Yi​=0)=0.64

A Bernoulli distribution describes one trial. It assigns all probability to the two possible outcomes.

Conditional mean and variance

E(Yi∣xi)=pi,Var⁡(Yi∣xi)=pi(1−pi)E(Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=p_i,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=p_i(1-p_i)E(Yi​∣xi​)=pi​,Var(Yi​∣xi​)=pi​(1−pi​)

E is expectation and Var is variance. These are conditional on the predictors. Variance is in squared outcome units; it is not a standard deviation.

E(Yi)=0.36,Var⁡(Yi)=0.36(0.64)=0.2304,SD⁡(Yi)=0.2304=0.48E(Y_i)=0.36,\quad\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=0.36(0.64)=0.2304,\quad\operatorname{SD}(Y_i)=\sqrt{0.2304}=0.48E(Yi​)=0.36,Var(Yi​)=0.36(0.64)=0.2304,SD(Yi​)=0.2304​=0.48

The model predicts an average of 0.36 successes per customer, not a fractional observed acceptance.

Bernoulli, binomial and generalized linear models

For m independent trials with a common success probability p, the number of successes S has a binomial distribution. Its mean is mp and variance mp(1−p). A Bernoulli variable is the special case m=1. For example, among 20 comparable customers with p=0.36, E(S)=20×0.36=7.2 and Var(S)=20×0.36×0.64=4.608. The actual number must still be an integer.

A generalized linear model (GLM) specifies a response distribution, a linear predictor η and a link connecting the response mean to η. Logistic regression uses a binomial response with the logit link; Poisson regression uses a Poisson response with the log link. The lecture calls this a “General Linear Model”; the standard expansion of GLM here is “generalized linear model”. The link acts on the conditional mean p, not on an individual observed y=0 or y=1, whose logit would be infinite.

When to use it and what to check

Use independent binary outcomes or properly specified binomial totals with numerical or categorical predictors. Repeated observations of the same person need dependence to be modeled; simply fitting an ordinary glm does not fix this. Check the coding of the event, missing values, plausible linearity of continuous predictors on the log-odds scale, and complete separation. There is no null hypothesis just to define a variable; coefficient hypotheses enter when fitting a regression.

  1. Identify the unit

    One bank customer is one observation. Income is a predictor measured in thousands of dollars; Personal.Loan is the response, 1=yes and 0=no.

  2. Separate outcome from probability

    A particular response is either 0 or 1. A model estimate p̂=0.36 describes the chance of 1 for a customer with that information.

  3. Choose a compatible model

    A binomial family with logit link keeps predictions between 0 and 1. A straight fitted line has no such guarantee.

  4. Interpret carefully

    An association between income and acceptance does not show that raising a person’s income causes acceptance. A probability estimate does not determine an individual’s future choice.

Self-check: If p=0.8, what is the variance of a binary response?

0.8×0.2=0.16. Its standard deviation is √0.16=0.4. A variance of 0.8 would confuse the conditional mean with the conditional variance.

Represent and inspect binary data in R

data.frame(), c() and str() belong to base R. stats::glm() and stats::binomial() are included with R and are loaded by default. No extra package is needed. An integer response coded 0/1 is unambiguous; with a factor response, verify which level is treated as success.

example <- data.frame(Income=c(49,34,11,100,180),
                      Personal.Loan=c(0L,0L,0L,0L,1L))
str(example)
table(example$Personal.Loan)
stopifnot(all(example$Personal.Loan %in% c(0,1)))
dbinom(1, size=1, prob=0.36)
20*0.36; 20*0.36*(1-0.36)
'data.frame': 5 obs. of 2 variables:
 $ Income       : num 49 34 11 100 180
 $ Personal.Loan: int 0 0 0 0 1
0 1
4 1
[1] 0.36
[1] 7.2
[1] 4.608
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
str(object)Displays the structure, column types and representative values; it does not fit a model.
dbinom(x, size, prob)Returns P(S=x); size=1 is Bernoulli, size=20 describes 20 trials.
%in% c(0,1)Checks that all observed response codes are allowed. Handle NA values explicitly before this check.

The table reports four non-acceptances and one acceptance in this small illustrative input. This is a coding exercise, not the bank’s fitted model. For grouped counts, use cbind(successes, failures) as the binomial response; never pass the successes alone without the trial totals.

# Copyable coding check
y <- c(0,1,0,0,1)
table(y)
mean(y)

The sample mean is 2/5=0.4 because the mean of a 0/1 vector is its observed success proportion. It is a descriptive estimate, not an adjusted regression prediction.

Probability, Odds and Log-Odds

Translate among three scales that describe the same chance: probability, odds and logit.

Lecture 3, slides 6–8

Three ways to describe a chance

Probability compares successes with all outcomes. Odds compare successes with failures. Log-odds take the natural logarithm of the odds, turning the positive odds scale into the whole real line. Logistic regression is linear on that last scale. A 75% rain probability means three rainy outcomes for every one non-rainy outcome, so odds are 3 to 1. It does not mean 75-to-1 odds.

Probability to odds

O=p1−pO=\frac{p}{1-p}O=1−pp​

p is the event probability; 1−p is its complement; O denotes odds. For 0

p=34:O=0.750.25=3p=\frac34:\quad O=\frac{0.75}{0.25}=3p=43​:O=0.250.75​=3

The event is three times as likely as its complement. This is a within-event comparison, not a comparison of two populations.

Odds to probability

p=O1+Op=\frac{O}{1+O}p=1+OO​

O is a nonnegative odds value and p is the resulting probability.

O=3:p=31+3=0.75O=3:\quad p=\frac3{1+3}=0.75O=3:p=1+33​=0.75

Add the success-to-failure ratio parts before dividing. Odds 3 do not imply probability 3.

Logit

η=logit⁡(p)=ln⁡ ⁣(p1−p)=ln⁡O\eta=\operatorname{logit}(p)=\ln\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\ln Oη=logit(p)=ln(1−pp​)=lnO

η (eta) is the log-odds; ln is the natural logarithm. The finite logit is defined for 0

p=0.75:η=ln⁡3=1.098612p=0.75:\quad\eta=\ln3=1.098612p=0.75:η=ln3=1.098612

A positive logit means p>0.5. Zero means p=0.5. A negative logit means p<0.5.

Inverse logit

O=eη,p=eη1+eη=11+e−ηO=e^\eta,\qquad p=\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}=\frac1{1+e^{-\eta}}O=eη,p=1+eηeη​=1+e−η1​

e is the base of natural logarithms. These inverse transformations recover the odds and probability from η.

η=1.098612:O≈3,p≈34=0.75\eta=1.098612:\quad O\approx3,\quad p\approx\frac34=0.75η=1.098612:O≈3,p≈43​=0.75

A fitted linear predictor can be any finite real number while its inverse-logit probability remains strictly between 0 and 1.

pOddsLogit
0.251/3−1.098612
0.5010
0.7531.098612

A complete conversion example

  1. Set the original information

    A forecast assigns rain probability 0.75. This is a transformation task; no hypothesis test or significance level is required.

  2. Compute the complement

    P(no rain)=1−0.75=0.25.

  3. Calculate odds

    0.75/0.25=3. There are three rainy outcomes per non-rainy outcome in the probabilistic description.

  4. Take the natural logarithm

    ln(3)=1.098612. If someone gives you this logit instead, exponentiate first: exp(1.098612)≈3.

  5. Reverse and check

    3/(1+3)=0.75. The recovered probability matches the original, which checks the direction of the conversion.

Boundary values

At p=0 the logit tends to −∞, and at p=1 it tends to +∞. The lecture’s ranges include these as limiting endpoints, not ordinary finite logits. Odds ratios are ratios of odds; they are generally not ratios of probabilities.

Self-check: What does a logit of −ln(3) imply?

Odds exp(−ln3)=1/3. The probability is (1/3)/(1+1/3)=1/4=0.25.

Convert scales with base R and stats

log() and exp() are base R. stats::qlogis() is the logit and stats::plogis() is its numerically stable inverse. No package installation is needed.

p <- 0.75
odds <- p/(1-p)
eta <- log(odds)
c(probability=p, odds=odds, logit=eta,
  recovered=plogis(eta))
qlogis(c(0.25,0.5,0.75))
probability        odds       logit   recovered
   0.750000    3.000000    1.098612    0.750000
[1] -1.098612  0.000000  1.098612
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
qlogis(p)p is a probability or vector of probabilities. Returns log(p/(1−p)); endpoints produce infinities.
plogis(q)q is a log-odds value, not an odds value. Returns a probability.
log(x, base=exp(1))The default is natural logarithm. Using log10() would change the link scale.

Each named output corresponds to one manual step. recovered verifies the inverse transformation. Changing p to 0.5 gives odds 1 and logit 0. Changing p to 0.25 gives odds 1/3 and a negative logit.

# Copyable conversion
p <- 0.75
c(odds=p/(1-p), logit=qlogis(p), check=plogis(qlogis(p)))

For probability 0.75, the odds are 3 and the log-odds are approximately 1.099; converting back returns 0.75.

The Logit Model

Connect predictors to log-odds, then transform the fitted line into an S-shaped probability curve.

Lecture 3, slides 4–10

The model and its purpose

A bank wants to target future loan mailings toward customers more likely to accept. Logistic regression lets income, age, account types and other predictors explain the probability of acceptance. The response remains binary; the fitted conditional mean is a probability. With just income, the model has an intercept and one slope.

Linear predictor and link

ηi=β0+∑j=1kβjxji,ln⁡pi1−pi=ηi\eta_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ji},\qquad \ln\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}=\eta_iηi​=β0​+j=1∑k​βj​xji​,ln1−pi​pi​​=ηi​

i indexes customers; j indexes predictors; k is their number; β₀ is the intercept; βⱼ is a slope; xⱼᵢ is predictor j for customer i; pᵢ is acceptance probability. Estimated coefficients are written with hats.

η^=−6.12731530+0.03712516(150)=−0.5585413\hat\eta=-6.12731530+0.03712516(150)=-0.5585413η^​=−6.12731530+0.03712516(150)=−0.5585413

The additive predictor describes log-odds. Income=150 means $150,000 because the source measures income in thousands.

Response-scale prediction

p^i=11+exp⁡(−η^i)\hat p_i=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-\hat\eta_i)}p^​i​=1+exp(−η^​i​)1​

p̂ᵢ is a fitted probability; η̂ᵢ is the fitted log-odds. The hat denotes an estimate from data.

p^=11+e0.5585413=0.3638850\hat p=\frac{1}{1+e^{0.5585413}}=0.3638850p^​=1+e0.55854131​=0.3638850

Comparable customers with $150,000 income have estimated acceptance probability about 36.4% under the displayed bank model.

The logistic curve flattens near probabilities 0 and 1 and changes fastest near 0.5. A constant change in income produces a constant change in log-odds, but not a constant change in probability. A categorical predictor can enter through indicator columns; its coefficient compares a category with a chosen reference category while holding other predictors fixed.

Assumptions, hypotheses and fitting

Assume independently sampled outcomes conditional on the predictors, a correctly specified logit mean, no exact redundant predictors, and sufficient information to estimate coefficients. Predictors need not themselves be normally distributed. A Bernoulli response need not have constant variance. Observational data support conditional associations; causal claims need a suitable design and further assumptions.

For a slope, the usual two-sided test is H0:βj=0H_0:\beta_j=0H0​:βj​=0 versus HA:βj≠0H_A:\beta_j\ne0HA​:βj​=0: no conditional log-odds association versus a nonzero one. A one-sided hypothesis such as βj>0\beta_j>0βj​>0 must be chosen for a substantive reason before looking at the result. Maximum likelihood finds coefficients that make the observed pattern of zeros and ones most likely; glm uses iterative numerical fitting.

Source data boundary

The lecture describes 5,000 bank customers, but Personal loan.csv was not supplied. Lecture coefficients and summary fields below are faithfully transcribed; they cannot be refitted from the PDF. A separate, fully declared grouped dataset makes the R procedure runnable. It does not reproduce the bank model.

From model to customer prediction

  1. Define the response and predictor

    Personal.Loan=1 means yes. Income is in $1,000 units. Use the lecture’s displayed coefficients, not newly fitted illustrative ones.

  2. Write the model

    η^=−6.12731530+0.03712516 Income\hat\eta=-6.12731530+0.03712516\,Incomeη^​=−6.12731530+0.03712516Income. There is one predictor, so no other values are needed for substitution.

  3. Multiply before adding

    0.03712516×150=5.568774. Then −6.12731530+5.568774=−0.55854130.

  4. Convert log-odds to odds

    e−0.55854130≈0.57204289e^{-0.55854130}\approx0.57204289e−0.55854130≈0.57204289. These odds are below 1, so the probability must be below 0.5.

  5. Convert odds to probability

    0.57204289/(1+0.57204289)=0.36388504. The probability is about 36.4%.

  6. State the practical meaning

    This is an estimated chance of acceptance for this income, not a promise that this individual accepts. It also does not estimate a causal effect of income.

Self-check: If η increases from −1 to 0, what happens?

The probability increases from plogis(−1)=0.26894 to plogis(0)=0.5. The odds multiply by e≈2.718. The probability does not multiply by e.

Fit a complete binomial GLM

stats::glm() performs maximum likelihood fitting for the specified GLM family. This runnable grouped illustration uses 20 trials at each of five income levels; it is not the original bank sample.

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
summary(logistic)
coef(logistic)
Coefficients (new illustrative data):
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -4.1039284  0.8045992  -5.101 3.386e-07
Income       0.0293076  0.0057042   5.138 2.778e-07
Null deviance: 41.818641 on 4 degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 0.012928 on 3 degrees of freedom
AIC: 18.38623
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
formula: cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ IncomeThe first column is successes, the second failures. Income is the predictor. For individual customers use Personal.Loan ~ Income with a 0/1 response.
data=CreditSearch for the formula variables inside the declared data frame.
family=binomial(link="logit")Use the binomial distribution and logit link. Changing to poisson() changes the statistical model, not just a display option.

The illustrative intercept and slope differ from the bank coefficients because these are different observations. Each z value is Estimate/Std. Error; the p-value tests the coefficient equal to zero under a large-sample normal approximation. The grouped residual degrees of freedom count five rows minus two fitted coefficients, not 100 trials minus two.

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
predict(logistic, newdata=data.frame(Income=150), type="response")
[1] 0.5725381

In this new illustrative model, the predicted acceptance probability at income 150 is about 57.3%. This is deliberately kept separate from the lecture model’s 36.4%.

Model Coefficients and Interpretation

Read estimates, standard errors, z-tests and odds ratios without confusing their scales.

Lecture 3, slides 13, 15–16

The bank model output

Source data boundary

The lecture describes 5,000 bank customers, but Personal loan.csv was not supplied. Lecture coefficients and summary fields below are faithfully transcribed; they cannot be refitted from the PDF. A separate, fully declared grouped dataset makes the R procedure runnable. It does not reproduce the bank model.

TermEstimateStd. ErrorzReported p
Intercept−6.1273150.186078−32.93<2×10⁻¹⁶
Income0.0371250.00137926.93<2×10⁻¹⁶

The estimate is a fitted coefficient. Its standard error describes uncertainty in that estimate under the fitted model; it is not the standard deviation of customer incomes or of their outcomes. The z value compares the coefficient with its standard error, and the p-value measures how extreme that standardized statistic would be under a zero-coefficient null hypothesis.

Change in log-odds

Δη=β1Δx\Delta\eta=\beta_1\Delta xΔη=β1​Δx

β₁ is the income slope, Δx is the change in income in $1,000 units, and Δη is the change in log-odds with other predictors held fixed.

Δx=1:Δη^=0.03712516(1)=0.03712516\Delta x=1:\quad\Delta\hat\eta=0.03712516(1)=0.03712516Δx=1:Δη^​=0.03712516(1)=0.03712516

A $1,000 increase changes fitted log-odds by about 0.03713. It does not increase probability by 0.03713.

Odds ratio

OR(Δx)=eβ1ΔxOR(\Delta x)=e^{\beta_1\Delta x}OR(Δx)=eβ1​Δx

OR is the ratio of odds after the predictor change to odds before it; exp converts a log-odds difference into an odds multiplier.

OR(1)=e0.03712516=1.0378229,100(OR−1)=3.78229%OR(1)=e^{0.03712516}=1.0378229,\quad100(OR-1)=3.78229\%OR(1)=e0.03712516=1.0378229,100(OR−1)=3.78229%

The exact fitted increase in odds per $1,000 is about 3.78%. The lecture’s 3.7% is a small-slope approximation. For $5,000 use exp(5β₁), rather than adding 3.78 percentage points to probability.

Coefficient z-test

z=β^j−βj,0SE(β^j),ptwo=2{1−Φ(∣z∣)}z=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_{j,0}}{SE(\hat\beta_j)},\quad p_{\mathrm{two}}=2\{1-\Phi(|z|)\}z=SE(β^​j​)β^​j​−βj,0​​,ptwo​=2{1−Φ(∣z∣)}

βⱼ,₀ is the value under H₀ (usually 0); SE is the coefficient’s standard error; Φ is the standard-normal cumulative distribution function. This is an asymptotic Wald test.

z≈0.0371250.001379=26.92z\approx\frac{0.037125}{0.001379}=26.92z≈0.0013790.037125​=26.92

The rounded inputs give about 26.92; R’s full-precision fit reports 26.93. Such a large |z| gives an extremely small two-sided p-value. It is not literally zero.

Approximate coefficient and odds-ratio intervals

β^j±1.96SE(β^j),CIOR=exp⁡(CIβ)\hat\beta_j\pm1.96SE(\hat\beta_j),\qquad CI_{OR}=\exp(CI_\beta)β^​j​±1.96SE(β^​j​),CIOR​=exp(CIβ​)

1.96 is the standard-normal 97.5th percentile for a two-sided approximate 95% Wald interval; exponentiate both endpoints separately.

0.037125±1.96(0.001379)=[0.0344222,0.0398278]0.037125\pm1.96(0.001379)=[0.0344222,0.0398278]0.037125±1.96(0.001379)=[0.0344222,0.0398278]

The corresponding odds-ratio interval is approximately [1.03502,1.04063]. This is a model-based interval, not a range of individual acceptance probabilities.

Hypotheses and context

At α=0.05\alpha=0.05α=0.05, reject H0:βIncome=0H_0:\beta_{Income}=0H0​:βIncome​=0 in favor of HA:βIncome≠0H_A:\beta_{Income}\ne0HA​:βIncome​=0. Income is positively associated with acceptance odds under this single-predictor model. This does not establish causation, rule out omitted predictors, guarantee good calibration, or make the effect constant on the probability scale.

  1. Identify the units

    One Income unit is $1,000, so a $1 change is Δx=0.001, not 1.

  2. Read the coefficient

    The fitted slope is 0.03712516 log-odds per Income unit.

  3. Exponentiate for an odds multiplier

    exp(0.03712516)=1.0378229. Subtract 1 and multiply by 100 to obtain 3.78229%.

  4. Assess uncertainty

    Use the coefficient SE and Wald test under its asymptotic assumptions. At p<2×10⁻¹⁶, the source model provides strong evidence of a nonzero slope.

  5. Explain the intercept

    At income zero, odds are exp(−6.12731530)=0.002182432. The intercept sets the curve’s position; income zero may lie outside the useful observed range.

Self-check: Does OR=2 mean the probability doubles?

No. Starting at p=0.2, odds are 0.25. Doubling gives odds 0.5 and probability 0.5/1.5=1/3, not 0.4.

Extract coefficients and transform them

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
co <- summary(logistic)$coefficients
co
exp(coef(logistic))
exp(cbind(estimate=coef(logistic),
          lower=coef(logistic)-1.96*sqrt(diag(vcov(logistic))),
          upper=coef(logistic)+1.96*sqrt(diag(vcov(logistic)))))
exp(coef(logistic)) — new illustrative fit:
(Intercept)      Income
 0.01650770  1.02974131
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
coef(model)Extracts named point estimates on the link scale.
summary(model)$coefficientsA matrix of estimates, standard errors, z values and p-values.
exp(coef(model))Exponentiates every coefficient, including the intercept. The intercept becomes baseline odds, not a slope odds ratio.
vcov(model)Estimated coefficient covariance matrix. Its diagonal contains coefficient variances; square roots give SEs.

These commands use base R/stats only. The interval code is a Wald interval; other interval methods can give different endpoints. In the illustrative data a one-unit income increase multiplies odds by 1.02974, about 2.97%, holding the model structure fixed.

# Copyable transformation of the lecture coefficients (no refit)
b <- c("(Intercept)"=-6.12731530, Income=0.03712516)
exp(b)
100*(exp(b["Income"])-1)
(Intercept)      Income
0.002182432 1.037822906
  Income
3.782291

The displayed lecture slope corresponds to a 3.78% increase in odds per additional $1,000 of income. This computation uses supplied coefficients directly; it does not recreate the bank data.

Logistic Predicted Probabilities

Follow a customer prediction through the linear predictor, odds and probability, and see why equal income changes have unequal probability effects.

Lecture 3, slides 9–10, 17

The bank prediction, with rounding made explicit

Use a fitted model when the new customer has predictor values measured and coded consistently with the training data. The lecture asks about incomes of $150,000 and $155,000. Neither question is a hypothesis test: the task is to compute and interpret a conditional mean.

  1. Write the inputs

    Use Income=150 or 155, β̂₀=−6.12731530 and β̂₁=0.03712516 from the displayed coefficient output.

  2. Calculate the log-odds at 150

    0.03712516×150=5.568774; −6.12731530+5.568774=−0.5585413.

  3. Exponentiate and convert

    Odds=exp(−0.5585413)=0.57204289. Probability=0.57204289/1.57204289=0.36388504.

  4. Repeat at 155

    0.03712516×155=5.7543998; η̂=−0.3729155. Probability=1/(1+exp(0.3729155))=0.40783672.

  5. Compare on the correct scale

    The probability change is 0.40783672−0.36388504=0.04395168, about 4.40 percentage points. The odds multiply by exp(5×0.03712516)=1.20397165, about a 20.40% increase in odds.

  6. Check the lecture rounding

    Slide 17 uses −6.13+0.037×Income. It gives p(150)=0.35893259 and p(155)=0.40251423, which round to 0.36 and 0.40. These are rounding differences, not contradictory fitted models.

  7. Interpret and limit the claim

    Both are estimated acceptance probabilities in the bank model. Neither is a guaranteed classification or causal effect. A classification cutoff, if needed, is a separate decision that depends on the costs of mistakes.

Logistic marginal effect (clarifying extension)

∂pi∂xji=βjpi(1−pi)\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial x_{ji}}=\beta_jp_i(1-p_i)∂xji​∂pi​​=βj​pi​(1−pi​)

βⱼ is a continuous predictor coefficient; pᵢ is its conditional probability. This derivative assumes no interaction or nonlinear transformation involving that predictor. It is additional clarification of the curve, not a separate lecture formula.

0.03712516(0.36388504)(1−0.36388504)≈0.008593460.03712516(0.36388504)(1-0.36388504)\approx0.008593460.03712516(0.36388504)(1−0.36388504)≈0.00859346

Near Income=150, an additional $1,000 corresponds locally to about 0.86 percentage points. The exact five-unit change must use two inverse-logit predictions, not five times a derivative assumed constant.

Prediction mistakes

Do not enter 150000 when the model expects thousands. Do not interpret type="link" as a probability. Do not round coefficients at every intermediate step. Predictions far outside the observed income range rely heavily on the chosen curve.

Self-check: At what η does the probability equal 0.5?

η=0, since exp(0)=1 and odds 1 correspond to p=1/(1+1)=0.5.

predict() versus direct substitution

stats::predict.glm() uses an already fitted glm. newdata supplies predictor values with matching column names. type="link" returns η̂ (the default), while type="response" returns probability for a binomial-logit model.

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
new <- data.frame(Income=c(150,155))
predict(logistic, newdata=new, type="link")
predict(logistic, newdata=new, type="response")
New illustrative fit:
Link:      0.2922140 0.4387521
Response:  0.5725381 0.6079616

These are predictions from the new grouped illustration. To reproduce the bank arithmetic without its missing CSV, explicitly use its published coefficients:

Income <- c(150,155)
eta <- -6.12731530+0.03712516*Income
data.frame(Income, eta, odds=exp(eta), probability=plogis(eta),
           rounded_model=plogis(-6.13+0.037*Income))
  Income        eta      odds probability rounded_model
1    150 -0.5585413 0.5720429   0.3638850     0.3589326
2    155 -0.3729155 0.6887234   0.4078367     0.4025142
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
newdata=data.frame(Income=...)Use the same predictor name and units. Categorical levels must match the fitted model.
type="response"Apply the inverse link; here it produces an acceptance probability.
type="link"Keep log-odds. For uncertainty, predict(..., se.fit=TRUE) can return a link-scale SE; transforming η±1.96SE gives an approximate probability interval.
# Copyable lecture prediction
income <- c(150,155)
plogis(-6.12731530+0.03712516*income)

Under the displayed bank model, acceptance probabilities are approximately 36.39% and 40.78% at incomes $150,000 and $155,000. Using rounded lecture coefficients gives the slide’s 0.36 and 0.40.

Diagnostics and McFadden Pseudo-R²

Read likelihood-based fit measures and understand the important condition behind the lecture’s deviance shortcut.

Lecture 3, slides 13–14

What the summary tells you

A model can have a very small coefficient p-value and still predict badly. Deviance compares fitted likelihood with a saturated model that reproduces each response as closely as the chosen family permits. Null deviance uses only an intercept; residual deviance uses the predictors. The word “residual” does not mean residual variance here.

GLM deviance

D=2(ℓsat−ℓfit)D=2(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_{\mathrm{fit}})D=2(ℓsat​−ℓfit​)

ℓ is the maximized log-likelihood; sat is the saturated model and fit is the model being assessed. Deviance is a discrepancy statistic, not a standard deviation.

D0=3162.0,D1=2016.2,D0−D1=1045.8D_0=3162.0,\quad D_1=2016.2,\quad D_0-D_1=1045.8D0​=3162.0,D1​=2016.2,D0​−D1​=1045.8

The bank predictor reduces deviance by 1045.8 compared with an intercept alone. A nested likelihood-ratio test compares this difference with χ² with the number of added parameters, here 1, under appropriate large-sample conditions.

Akaike Information Criterion

AIC=−2ℓfit+2qAIC=-2\ell_{\mathrm{fit}}+2qAIC=−2ℓfit​+2q

q is the number of fitted parameters counted by the model. Compare AIC only across fits to the same response observations and comparable likelihoods; smaller is preferred as a relative tradeoff, not an absolute guarantee.

q=2,AIC=2016.2+2(2)=2020.2q=2,\quad AIC=2016.2+2(2)=2020.2q=2,AIC=2016.2+2(2)=2020.2

For individual Bernoulli observations ℓsat=0, so the lecture’s −2ℓ equals deviance. This equality does not hold for every GLM or every binomial grouping.

McFadden pseudo-R²

RMcF2=1−ℓfitℓnullR^2_{\mathrm{McF}}=1-\frac{\ell_{\mathrm{fit}}}{\ell_{\mathrm{null}}}RMcF2​=1−ℓnull​ℓfit​​

The null fit is intercept-only and must use the same observations. Both log-likelihoods are typically negative. This is a relative likelihood measure, not a fraction of outcome variance explained.

1−2016.23162.0=0.36236561-\frac{2016.2}{3162.0}=0.36236561−3162.02016.2​=0.3623656

Using the rounded lecture deviances gives 0.3623656; the full-precision lecture calculation reports 0.3623641. The small difference is rounding.

When the deviance ratio is valid

The lecture writes null.deviance=−2ln(Lnull) and residual.deviance=−2ln(Lmodel). That shortcut works for individual 0/1 Bernoulli observations with saturated log-likelihood zero. In grouped binomial data or Poisson counts the saturated log-likelihood generally is not zero. Compute McFadden directly with logLik() instead of blindly taking 1−D1/D0.

Read every bank summary field

  1. Count the observations and parameters

    Null df=4999 implies 5000 individual observations. Residual df=4998 implies two fitted coefficients, the intercept and Income.

  2. Compare model fit

    Null deviance 3162.0 falls to residual deviance 2016.2. Reduction=3162.0−2016.2=1045.8.

  3. Account for complexity

    AIC=2016.2+2×2=2020.2 for this individual Bernoulli model.

  4. Compute the pseudo-R²

    2016.2/3162.0=0.6376344; 1−0.6376344=0.3623656 using rounded fields.

  5. Inspect what remains untested

    The summary’s deviance residual quantiles are Min −2.1424, 1Q −0.3048, Median −0.1760, 3Q −0.1130, Max 2.7999. They summarize residual asymmetry and extremes; they do not alone establish adequate calibration or identify influential cases.

  6. Read fitting details

    Binomial dispersion is fixed at 1 by the specified family. Six Fisher scoring iterations means six numerical fitting updates, not six observations or six predictors. Check convergence warnings and unusual fitted values.

Useful further diagnostics include plotting binned observed acceptance rates against predicted probabilities, examining influence and residuals, and checking performance on held-out data. None can be verified for the original bank sample without its CSV. A pseudo-R² of 0.362 does not mean that 36.2% of individual choices have been explained or that 63.8% were misclassified.

Self-check: Can you compare AIC from models fitted after different NA deletions?

Not directly as a like-for-like predictor comparison. Refit both on the same complete observations first.

Compute fit measures without misusing a shortcut

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
null <- update(logistic, . ~ 1)
c(null_deviance=logistic$null.deviance,
  residual_deviance=deviance(logistic), AIC=AIC(logistic),
  deviance_ratio=1-deviance(logistic)/logistic$null.deviance,
  McFadden=1-as.numeric(logLik(logistic))/as.numeric(logLik(null)))
New grouped illustrative data:
null_deviance      41.81864147
residual_deviance   0.01292761
AIC               18.38623179
deviance_ratio     0.99969086
McFadden           0.74398054

The very different final two values are intentional: this grouped dataset has nonzero saturated log-likelihood. It demonstrates why the bank’s convenient formula must not be applied indiscriminately.

Argument / functionMeaning and choices
update(model, . ~ 1)Retains the response and data while replacing predictors by an intercept. Ensure it uses the same observations when missing predictor values exist.
deviance(), model$null.devianceReturn residual and null deviance. They are not log-likelihoods themselves.
logLik(), AIC()Return the model’s log-likelihood and information criterion. as.numeric() removes logLik’s metadata for arithmetic.
# Copyable arithmetic from the lecture's rounded bank summary
1-2016.2/3162.0
2016.2+2*2
[1] 0.3623656
[1] 2020.2

The bank model improves likelihood relative to an intercept-only model. McFadden’s pseudo-R² is about 0.362; it is not ordinary linear-regression R².

Logistic Regression in R

A complete import-to-interpretation workflow, with the original lecture pipeline and a separate runnable example.

Lecture 3, slides 9, 11–17

Loading and inspecting the bank data

Source data boundary

The lecture describes 5,000 bank customers, but Personal loan.csv was not supplied. Lecture coefficients and summary fields below are faithfully transcribed; they cannot be refitted from the PDF. A separate, fully declared grouped dataset makes the R procedure runnable. It does not reproduce the bank model.

The original CSV is a prerequisite for the next source-specific block. read.csv() reads a local file; str() checks what was loaded. Default check.names=TRUE converts spaces in column names to dots, explaining Personal.Loan. The 14 source columns are ID, Age, Experience, Income, ZIP.Code, Family, CCAvg, Education, Mortgage, Personal.Loan, Securities.Account, CD.Account, Online and CreditCard.

# Original lecture workflow: requires the unprovided source CSV.
Credit <- read.csv("Personal loan.csv")
str(Credit)
logistic <- glm(Personal.Loan ~ Income, data=Credit,
                family=binomial(link="logit"))
summary(logistic)
coef(logistic)
exp(coef(logistic))
predict(logistic, newdata=data.frame(Income=c(150,155)),
        type="response")

Lecture-reported str() shows 5,000 observations and 14 variables: CCAvg is numeric and the displayed other columns are integers. The first ten Income values are 49,34,11,100,45,29,72,22,81,180; the first ten Personal.Loan values are nine zeros followed by 1. This excerpt is for checking the import, not enough data to recreate the fit. The scatterplot on slide 12 has responses in two horizontal bands at 0 and 1, as expected for a binary outcome.

Complete runnable replacement demonstration

# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
str(Credit)
summary(logistic)
exp(coef(logistic))
predict(logistic, newdata=data.frame(Income=c(100,150,155)),
        type="response")
New illustrative fit:
Coefficients: (Intercept)=-4.10392843, Income=0.02930762
SE:             0.80459925          0.00570416
z:             -5.10058695          5.13793676
p:              3.3860e-07          2.7777e-07
Predictions at Income 100,150,155:
0.2362831 0.5725381 0.6079616

The math connection is η̂=−4.10392843+0.02930762×Income followed by plogis(η̂). At 150 this gives η̂=0.29221404 and p̂=0.57253808. Estimate is on the logit scale, SE measures coefficient uncertainty, z divides the two, and the p-value tests a zero coefficient.

Plot the logistic probability curve

The lecture draws random p values with runif(1000), computes log(p/(1−p)) and uses ggplot2::geom_line(). A deterministic grid makes the same mathematical relationship easier to reproduce. ggplot2 is optional and requires installation once; the guide itself needs neither R nor packages to display its own interactive curve.

# Optional graph; install.packages("ggplot2") once if needed.
library(ggplot2)
p <- seq(0.001,0.999,length.out=1000)
LR <- data.frame(probability=p, logit=qlogis(p))
ggplot(LR, aes(x=logit, y=probability))+geom_line()

aes maps columns to axes; geom_line connects the points in x order. The S-curve crosses probability 0.5 at logit 0 and approaches its limits smoothly. The original slide uses aes(y=p) with p available externally; using y=probability makes the column dependency explicit.

Self-check: Why does glm(cbind(successes, failures) ~ x) not have df equal to total trials minus two?

The grouped fit has one binomial response row per predictor pattern. Its residual degrees of freedom count grouped rows minus fitted coefficients.

Functions, arguments and a copyable exam answer

Argument / functionMeaning and choices
read.csv(file, header=TRUE)file is a local path; header indicates that the first row contains names. A wrong working directory causes a missing-file error.

predict(object, newdata, type)For binomial-logit fits, response means probabilities; link means log-odds.
# New illustrative grouped dataset; not the bank's 5,000 customers.
Credit <- data.frame(Income=c(40,80,120,160,200),
                     accepted=c(1,3,7,13,17), trials=rep(20,5))
logistic <- glm(cbind(accepted, trials-accepted) ~ Income,
                data=Credit, family=binomial(link="logit"))
print(summary(logistic)$coefficients)
print(predict(logistic,newdata=data.frame(Income=150),type="response"))

For the explicitly illustrative grouped data, income has a positive fitted slope of about 0.0293, and its large-sample Wald p-value is about 2.78×10⁻⁷. At Income=150 the fitted acceptance probability is about 0.573. These statements refer only to this new demonstration. The lecture bank model and its different values remain separately documented.

Count Data and the Poisson Distribution

Model nonnegative integer counts with a positive conditional mean and a distribution that assigns probabilities to individual counts.

Lecture 3, slides 18–20

Why count data need a count model

Counts are 0,1,2,…: doctor visits per year, fishing trips, children, accidents per month, televisions in a household and weekly drinks are the lecture examples. A count is not a continuous amount and is not restricted to 0/1. A linear model can predict impossible negative expected counts; a binary model throws away information when more than one event is possible.

Use a Poisson model when counts refer to a clearly defined observation unit and exposure, observations are conditionally independent, and the conditional mean–variance relationship is plausible. Equal means and variances refer to counts with the same predictors, not automatically the mixture of every country or person. Unequal observation times require an exposure adjustment. Excess variation and excess zeros are diagnostic questions, not proof that every count variable follows a Poisson distribution.

Poisson probability mass function

P(Y=y∣λ)=e−λλyy!,y=0,1,2,…P(Y=y\mid\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!},\quad y=0,1,2,\ldotsP(Y=y∣λ)=y!e−λλy​,y=0,1,2,…

Y is the count; y is a possible observed integer; λ>0 is its mean; y! is y factorial with 0!=1. This is a probability mass, not a density or an expected count.

λ=2, y=2:P(Y=2)=e−2222!=0.1353353(4)2=0.2706706\lambda=2,\ y=2:\quad P(Y=2)=\frac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}=\frac{0.1353353(4)}2=0.2706706λ=2, y=2:P(Y=2)=2!e−222​=20.1353353(4)​=0.2706706

A process with expected count 2 has about 27.1% probability of exactly two events. It does not produce exactly two every time.

Mean, variance and standard deviation

E(Y∣x)=λ,Var⁡(Y∣x)=λ,SD⁡(Y∣x)=λE(Y\mid\mathbf x)=\lambda,\quad\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathbf x)=\lambda,\quad\operatorname{SD}(Y\mid\mathbf x)=\sqrt\lambdaE(Y∣x)=λ,Var(Y∣x)=λ,SD(Y∣x)=λ​

Expectation and variance share the same numerical parameter in a Poisson distribution; SD is their square-root scale, not λ itself.

λ=2:E(Y)=2,Var⁡(Y)=2,SD⁡(Y)=2=1.414214\lambda=2:\quad E(Y)=2,\quad\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2,\quad\operatorname{SD}(Y)=\sqrt2=1.414214λ=2:E(Y)=2,Var(Y)=2,SD(Y)=2​=1.414214

The equality of conditional mean and variance is an assumption worth assessing after fitting.

Upper-tail probability

P(Y≥2)=1−P(Y=0)−P(Y=1)P(Y\ge2)=1-P(Y=0)-P(Y=1)P(Y≥2)=1−P(Y=0)−P(Y=1)

A tail sums probability masses. Subtract the counts strictly below 2 from 1.

λ=2:1−e−2−2e−2=1−3(0.1353353)=0.5939942\lambda=2:\quad1-e^{-2}-2e^{-2}=1-3(0.1353353)=0.5939942λ=2:1−e−2−2e−2=1−3(0.1353353)=0.5939942

There is about a 59.4% chance of at least two events. At least two includes exactly two.

Poisson regression with a log link

Conditional mean model

log⁡λi=β1+β2xi,λi=eβ1+β2xi\log\lambda_i=\beta_1+\beta_2x_i,\qquad\lambda_i=e^{\beta_1+\beta_2x_i}logλi​=β1​+β2​xi​,λi​=eβ1​+β2​xi​

The lecture uses β₁ for the intercept and β₂ for a slope here; logistic sections use β₀ and β₁ instead. i indexes observations, xᵢ is the predictor and λᵢ is its conditional expected count.

β1=ln⁡2, β2=ln⁡1.5, x=1:λ=eln⁡2+ln⁡1.5=3\beta_1=\ln2,\ \beta_2=\ln1.5,\ x=1:\quad\lambda=e^{\ln2+\ln1.5}=3β1​=ln2, β2​=ln1.5, x=1:λ=eln2+ln1.5=3

This explicitly illustrative coefficient choice gives expected counts 2 at x=0 and 3 at x=1. Exponentiation keeps the fitted mean positive.

  1. Define a count and its interval

    Suppose Y counts visits per person-year. Compare equal exposure periods, or include an offset for different periods.

  2. Specify a mean

    For a simple probability calculation let λ=2. No hypothesis test is needed merely to evaluate the PMF.

  3. Calculate individual masses

    P(0)=exp(−2)=0.1353353; P(1)=exp(−2)×2=0.2706706; P(2)=exp(−2)×4/2=0.2706706.

  4. Form the requested event

    P(Y≥2)=1−0.1353353−0.2706706=0.5939942.

  5. Interpret in the original unit

    Expected visits are 2 per person-year, with probability about 0.594 of at least two visits. Do not report 2 as a probability.

Self-check: Can the expected count be 0.96?

Yes. An expectation is an average, so it need not be an integer. Individual observed counts are integers.

Poisson functions in stats

stats::dpois() returns individual masses; stats::ppois() returns cumulative tails. Both are included with R. lambda is a nonnegative mean; use the same units/exposure as the intended count.

lambda <- 2
dpois(0:2, lambda=lambda)
ppois(1, lambda=lambda, lower.tail=FALSE)
c(mean=lambda, variance=lambda, SD=sqrt(lambda))
[1] 0.1353353 0.2706706 0.2706706
[1] 0.5939942
    mean variance       SD
2.000000 2.000000 1.414214
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
dpois(x, lambda)x is the count value or vector. Returns P(Y=x).
ppois(q, lambda, lower.tail=TRUE)Default returns P(Y≤q). lower.tail=FALSE returns P(Y>q), so at least 2 uses q=1, not q=2.
poisson(link="log")Defines a count GLM with positive mean exp(η). It is a family specification, not a fitted model by itself.
# Copyable count-probability answer
lambda <- 2
c(exactly_two=dpois(2,lambda), at_least_two=ppois(1,lambda,lower.tail=FALSE))

With mean two events per unit, the probability of exactly two is 0.2707 and of at least two is 0.5940. These are distribution calculations under the stated Poisson assumption.

Poisson Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Build the likelihood from the observed counts, take logs, derive score equations and follow a numerical fitting example.

Lecture 3, slides 21–22

What maximum likelihood does

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) chooses coefficients that assign the largest joint probability to the observed data under the model. It does not maximize the probability of every possible dataset simultaneously. Multiplication of independent probability masses gives the likelihood; taking logs replaces the product by a sum without changing which coefficients maximize it.

Missing predictors in the lecture

Slides 21–22 provide counts y=(0,2,2), but no observed x values. That is enough to write a symbolic likelihood, not enough to estimate a numerical intercept and slope. We retain the symbolic derivation first. A fully solved numerical extension explicitly introduces x=(0,1,2); those x values are new teaching data, not recovered source observations.

Likelihood

L(β1,β2)=∏i=1ne−λiλiyiyi!,λi=eβ1+β2xiL(\beta_1,\beta_2)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\lambda_i}\lambda_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},\quad\lambda_i=e^{\beta_1+\beta_2x_i}L(β1​,β2​)=i=1∏n​yi​!e−λi​λiyi​​​,λi​=eβ1​+β2​xi​

n is the number of independent observations; yᵢ and xᵢ are observed response and predictor values; λᵢ is their fitted mean; β₁,β₂ are unknown coefficients.

y=(0,2,2):L=e−(λ1+λ2+λ3)λ22λ320! 2! 2!=e−∑iλiλ22λ324y=(0,2,2):\quad L=\frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3)}\lambda_2^2\lambda_3^2}{0!\,2!\,2!}=\frac{e^{-\sum_i\lambda_i}\lambda_2^2\lambda_3^2}{4}y=(0,2,2):L=0!2!2!e−(λ1​+λ2​+λ3​)λ22​λ32​​=4e−∑i​λi​λ22​λ32​​

The observation with zero events still contributes exp(−λ₁). Do not delete zero counts or invent a common mean when predictor values differ.

Log-likelihood

ℓ(β)=∑i=1n[−eβ1+β2xi+yi(β1+β2xi)−log⁡(yi!)]\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n[-e^{\beta_1+\beta_2x_i}+y_i(\beta_1+\beta_2x_i)-\log(y_i!)]ℓ(β)=i=1∑n​[−eβ1​+β2​xi​+yi​(β1​+β2​xi​)−log(yi​!)]

ℓ=log L; the factorial term depends on the observed count but not on the coefficients. Every term carries its own i-index.

x=(0,1,2), y=(0,2,2):ℓ=−eβ1−eβ1+β2−eβ1+2β2+4β1+6β2−2log⁡2x=(0,1,2),\ y=(0,2,2):\quad\ell=-e^{\beta_1}-e^{\beta_1+\beta_2}-e^{\beta_1+2\beta_2}+4\beta_1+6\beta_2-2\log2x=(0,1,2), y=(0,2,2):ℓ=−eβ1​−eβ1​+β2​−eβ1​+2β2​+4β1​+6β2​−2log2

The new illustrative x values allow actual substitution. The −2log2 term comes from log(0!)+log(2!)+log(2!).

Intercept score equation

∂ℓ∂β1=∑i(yi−λi)=0\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_1}=\sum_i(y_i-\lambda_i)=0∂β1​∂ℓ​=i∑​(yi​−λi​)=0

A score is a partial derivative of log-likelihood. The intercept score balances total fitted counts with total observed counts.

4−(λ1+λ2+λ3)=04-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3)=04−(λ1​+λ2​+λ3​)=0

At the maximum, these three fitted means sum to 4, provided the ordinary finite intercept model has converged.

Slope score equation

∂ℓ∂β2=∑ixi(yi−λi)=0\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_2}=\sum_i x_i(y_i-\lambda_i)=0∂β2​∂ℓ​=i∑​xi​(yi​−λi​)=0

Differentiate the exponential using the chain rule; xᵢ multiplies the residual contribution for the slope.

6−(λ2+2λ3)=06-(\lambda_2+2\lambda_3)=06−(λ2​+2λ3​)=0

The slope balances predictor-weighted counts. These equations are nonlinear in β; a general Poisson regression is solved numerically.

Curvature and a numerical update

g=X⊤(y−λ),∇2ℓ=−X⊤WX,βnew=β+(X⊤WX)−1g\mathbf g=X^\top(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\lambda),\quad\nabla^2\ell=-X^\top W X,\quad\boldsymbol\beta_{new}=\boldsymbol\beta+(X^\top W X)^{-1}\mathbf gg=X⊤(y−λ),∇2ℓ=−X⊤WX,βnew​=β+(X⊤WX)−1g

X has rows (1,xᵢ); g is the score vector; W is diagonal with λᵢ entries. Negative curvature supports maximization when the design has full rank. This is a Newton/Fisher scoring update for the canonical log link.

β(0)=(0,0):g=(1,3)⊤,X⊤WX=(3335),Δβ=(−2/3,1)⊤\boldsymbol\beta^{(0)}=(0,0):\quad\mathbf g=(1,3)^\top,\quad X^\top W X=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix},\quad\Delta\boldsymbol\beta=(-2/3,1)^\topβ(0)=(0,0):g=(1,3)⊤,X⊤WX=(33​35​),Δβ=(−2/3,1)⊤

Starting means are (1,1,1). The first update is (−0.666667,1), not the final answer; repeat with the updated means until convergence.

A fully solved illustrative extension

  1. Declare all observations

    ix (new extension)y (lecture counts)
    100
    212
    322

  2. State the estimation problem

    Assume independent Poisson counts with log λᵢ=β₁+β₂xᵢ. We are estimating coefficients rather than testing a null; no significance level is needed for maximization.

  3. Use the score equations

    Let a=exp(β₁) and r=exp(β₂). Then λ=(a,ar,ar²). The two score equations are a(1+r+r²)=4 and a(r+2r²)=6.

  4. Eliminate a

    a=4/(1+r+r2)a=4/(1+r+r^2)a=4/(1+r+r2). Substituting gives 4(r+2r2)=6(1+r+r2)4(r+2r^2)=6(1+r+r^2)4(r+2r2)=6(1+r+r2), hence r2−r−3=0r^2-r-3=0r2−r−3=0. The positive root is r=(1+13)/2=2.30277564r=(1+\sqrt{13})/2=2.30277564r=(1+13​)/2=2.30277564.

  5. Recover the parameters

    a=4/(1+r+r²)=0.46481624. β̂₁=ln(a)=−0.76611313 and β̂₂=ln(r)=0.83411519. This small designed extension admits algebraic elimination; general data still require numerical fitting.

  6. Check fitted means

    λ̂₁=0.46481624, λ̂₂=1.07036752, λ̂₃=2.46481624. Their sum is 4.000000; λ̂₂+2λ̂₃=6.000000, satisfying both scores up to rounding.

  7. Evaluate the objective

    Individual log masses are −0.46481624, −1.62751057, −1.35372891. Sum ℓ̂=−3.44605572; L̂=exp(ℓ̂)≈0.03187110. These values belong only to the extension.

  8. Explain the result

    The fitted expected count multiplies by exp(β̂₂)=2.3028 per x unit. The three observed counts need not equal the three fitted means. A zero observed count does not imply a zero fitted mean.

Self-check: What if only an intercept were estimated from y=(0,2,2)?

Then a single common mean is identifiable: λ^=yˉ=4/3\hat\lambda=\bar y=4/3λ^=yˉ​=4/3 and the log-intercept is ln(4/3). This is a different, intercept-only model; it cannot supply a missing slope.

Fit and verify the likelihood in R

stats::glm() performs iterative fitting. dpois(...,log=TRUE) evaluates log probability masses directly and avoids underflow from multiplying very small probabilities. All required data are declared here.

# Explicit illustrative extension: x was not supplied in the lecture.
demo <- data.frame(x=c(0,1,2), y=c(0,2,2))
fit <- glm(y~x, family=poisson(link="log"), data=demo)
coef(fit)
mu <- fitted(fit)
cbind(demo, mean=mu, log_mass=dpois(demo$y,mu,log=TRUE))
c(score_intercept=sum(demo$y-mu),
  score_slope=sum(demo$x*(demo$y-mu)),
  log_likelihood=sum(dpois(demo$y,mu,log=TRUE)))
(Intercept)           x
 -0.7661131   0.8341152
  x y      mean   log_mass
1 0 0 0.4648162 -0.4648162
2 1 2 1.0703675 -1.6275106
3 2 2 2.4648162 -1.3537289
Scores approximately 0, 0
log_likelihood = -3.4460557
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
family=poisson(link="log")The PMF is Poisson; its conditional mean is exp(linear predictor).
fitted(fit)Returns response-scale fitted means, not the link values.
dpois(y, mu, log=TRUE)Uses each observed count and its own mean to return a vector of log masses. sum() produces the log-likelihood.
logLik(fit)Returns the fitted log-likelihood, with metadata; agrees with the independently summed log masses.
demo <- data.frame(x=c(0,1,2),y=c(0,2,2))
fit <- glm(y~x,data=demo,family=poisson())
coef(fit)
logLik(fit)

In this explicit illustrative extension, the fitted intercept is −0.7661 and slope 0.8341. The model maximizes the stated Poisson likelihood and its fitted means satisfy the two score equations.

Conditional Mean and Count Predictions

A Poisson regression predicts an expected count first; individual count probabilities require one more step.

Lecture 3, slides 20, 23

Expected count versus probability

Suppose an illustrative model has intercept ln2 and slope ln1.5. At x=1 it predicts λ=3. This does not say that every observation equals 3, nor that the chance of an event is 3. A probability is obtained by putting this λ into the Poisson mass or tail formula. Prediction assumes the model and exposure unit are appropriate for the new observation.

Predict the conditional mean

λ^0=exp⁡(β^1+β^2x0)\hat\lambda_0=\exp(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2x_0)λ^0​=exp(β^​1​+β^​2​x0​)

The subscript 0 denotes a new observation; x₀ is its predictor; β̂₁ is the intercept and β̂₂ is the slope.

x0=1:λ^0=exp⁡(ln⁡2+ln⁡1.5)=3x_0=1:\quad\hat\lambda_0=\exp(\ln2+\ln1.5)=3x0​=1:λ^0​=exp(ln2+ln1.5)=3

The expected number of events is three in the observation interval. The mean may be fractional for other x values.

Predict a particular count probability

P^(Y0=y)=e−λ^0λ^0yy!\widehat{P}(Y_0=y)=\frac{e^{-\hat\lambda_0}\hat\lambda_0^y}{y!}P(Y0​=y)=y!e−λ^0​λ^0y​​

y is the particular nonnegative integer whose probability is requested. The hat signals that λ is estimated rather than known.

y=2, λ^0=3:P^(Y0=2)=e−392=0.2240418y=2,\ \hat\lambda_0=3:\quad\widehat{P}(Y_0=2)=e^{-3}\frac{9}{2}=0.2240418y=2, λ^0​=3:P(Y0​=2)=e−329​=0.2240418

The fitted probability of exactly two events is about 22.4%. This is distinct from the expected count 3.

  1. Write all predictor values

    For this one-predictor illustration take x₀=1. The coefficients ln2 and ln1.5 are illustrative, not estimated from the Olympic dataset.

  2. Calculate the link value

    ln2+ln1.5=ln3=1.0986123.

  3. Convert to the mean

    exp(1.0986123)=3.

  4. Specify the event

    Exactly two requires y=2: y!=2×1=2 and λ²=9.

  5. Evaluate the mass

    exp(−3)×9/2=0.04978707×4.5=0.22404181.

  6. If requested, calculate a tail

    P(Y≥2)=1−P(0)−P(1)=1−exp(−3)(1+3)=0.80085173.

  7. Conclude in context

    The model predicts 3 events on average, with approximately 22.4% chance of exactly two and 80.1% chance of at least two. These are plug-in predictions under Poisson assumptions, not prediction intervals.

Keep scales separate

For a Poisson glm, type="response" returns λ, which can exceed 1. It does not return a probability. Parameter uncertainty and the variability of a future count are different sources of uncertainty; a confidence interval for λ is not a prediction interval for a future Y.

Self-check: What is the probability of zero when λ=3?

exp(−3)×3⁰/0!=exp(−3)=0.0497871.

Compute the mean and then a mass or tail

# Standalone prediction using declared illustrative coefficients.
b0 <- log(2); b1 <- log(1.5); x0 <- 1
eta <- b0+b1*x0
lambda <- exp(eta)
c(link=eta, expected_count=lambda, exactly_two=dpois(2,lambda),
  at_least_two=ppois(1,lambda,lower.tail=FALSE))
          link expected_count     exactly_two    at_least_two
     1.0986123      3.0000000      0.2240418      0.8008517
Argument / functionMeaning and choices
exp(eta)Transforms log-mean into mean. For a fitted glm, predict(fit,newdata,type="response") does this transformation.
dpois(2,lambda)Mass at exactly two events; use the predicted λ, not the linear predictor η.
ppois(1,lambda,lower.tail=FALSE)Probability of strictly more than 1, equal to at least 2.
lambda <- exp(log(2)+log(1.5)*1)
c(mean=lambda, P0=dpois(0,lambda), P2=dpois(2,lambda))

For x=1 in the declared illustrative model, the fitted mean is 3, the zero-count probability is about 0.0498 and the probability of exactly two is about 0.2240.

Poisson Coefficients and Marginal Effects

Translate log-mean slopes into count multipliers, local derivatives and elasticities for logged predictors.

Lecture 3, slides 24, 27–28

Why the predictor scale matters

For an untransformed predictor in log λ=β₁+β₂x, one more x unit multiplies the expected count by exp(β₂). The marginal effect asks how fast the expected count changes at a particular x, and therefore depends on the current mean. When the predictor is log(GDP), the coefficient has a different interpretation: it is an elasticity, not a per-billion-dollar additive change.

Finite change for an unlogged predictor

λ(x+Δx)λ(x)=eβ2Δx\frac{\lambda(x+\Delta x)}{\lambda(x)}=e^{\beta_2\Delta x}λ(x)λ(x+Δx)​=eβ2​Δx

Δx is a predictor change in its original units; β₂ is the corresponding slope.

β2=ln⁡1.5, Δx=1:eln⁡1.5=1.5\beta_2=\ln1.5,\ \Delta x=1:\quad e^{\ln1.5}=1.5β2​=ln1.5, Δx=1:eln1.5=1.5

The illustrative expected count rises 50% per additional x unit. This compares means, not individual count probabilities.

Local marginal effect

∂E(Yi∣xi)∂xi=β2λi\frac{\partial E(Y_i\mid x_i)}{\partial x_i}=\beta_2\lambda_i∂xi​∂E(Yi​∣xi​)​=β2​λi​

λᵢ is the conditional mean at the chosen xᵢ. A derivative is a local rate in count units per predictor unit.

λi=3, β2=ln⁡1.5:3ln⁡1.5=1.216395\lambda_i=3,\ \beta_2=\ln1.5:\quad3\ln1.5=1.216395λi​=3, β2​=ln1.5:3ln1.5=1.216395

At x=1 in the illustrative model, the local slope is about 1.216 events per x unit. The exact change from x=1 to x=2 is 4.5−3=1.5, so the derivative and a full one-unit change differ.

Logged predictors and elasticity

log⁡λ=β0+βGlog⁡G+βPlog⁡P,∂log⁡λ∂log⁡G=βG,∂λ∂G=βGλG\log\lambda=\beta_0+\beta_G\log G+\beta_P\log P,\quad\frac{\partial\log\lambda}{\partial\log G}=\beta_G,\quad\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial G}=\beta_G\frac\lambda Glogλ=β0​+βG​logG+βP​logP,∂logG∂logλ​=βG​,∂G∂λ​=βG​Gλ​

G is GDP and P is population in the model’s positive units; βG and βP are their log-predictor coefficients. β₀ is the intercept in this multi-predictor notation.

G=5.79, λ=0.96116467:∂λ∂G=0.5700860.961164675.79≈0.0946367G=5.79,\ \lambda=0.96116467:\quad\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial G}=0.570086\frac{0.96116467}{5.79}\approx0.0946367G=5.79, λ=0.96116467:∂G∂λ​=0.5700865.790.96116467​≈0.0946367

A 1% increase in GDP is associated with approximately a 0.5701% increase in expected medals, holding population fixed. The derivative is about 0.0946 expected medals per extra GDP billion locally.

Exact percent change for a logged predictor

λ(Gnew)λ(Gold)=(GnewGold)βG\frac{\lambda(G_{new})}{\lambda(G_{old})}=\left(\frac{G_{new}}{G_{old}}\right)^{\beta_G}λ(Gold​)λ(Gnew​)​=(Gold​Gnew​​)βG​

The ratio uses the same GDP units in numerator and denominator and keeps other predictors fixed.

Gnew=1.01Gold:100(1.010.570086−1)≈0.56887%G_{new}=1.01G_{old}:\quad100(1.01^{0.570086}-1)\approx0.56887\%Gnew​=1.01Gold​:100(1.010.570086−1)≈0.56887%

This exact finite change is close to the elasticity approximation for a small 1% increase. For large changes, use the ratio expression.

Interpreting the Olympic coefficients

  1. Identify the model terms

    The lecture fits log(gdp) and log(pop). Their coefficients are 0.570086 and 0.207963, both positive.

  2. Choose a comparison

    Hold GDP fixed and increase population from 5.35 to 16.75 million.

  3. Form the mean ratio

    (16.75/5.35)0.207963=1.26788293(16.75/5.35)^{0.207963}=1.26788293(16.75/5.35)0.207963=1.26788293. Thus the expected count rises about 26.79%, according to the displayed coefficients.

  4. Connect with actual means

    The independently computed means are 0.96116467 and 1.21864427. Their ratio is 1.26788293. These do not equal the two reported slide-28 means.

  5. Explain the limits

    The coefficients describe a conditional association in country-year data. They do not establish that population growth or higher GDP causes medals; repeated countries and omitted country effects can matter for inference.

Self-check: Why does a negative Poisson coefficient imply a negative marginal effect?

For a finite log-link predictor λ is positive, so the product β₂λ has the same sign as β₂.

Compute derivatives and finite changes

These calculations use base R and the lecture’s displayed coefficients; they need no CSV or extra package.

gdp <- 5.79; pop <- 5.35
b <- c(intercept=-1.389530, log_gdp=0.570086, log_pop=0.207963)
lambda <- exp(b[1]+b[2]*log(gdp)+b[3]*log(pop))
c(mean=lambda, GDP_derivative=b[2]*lambda/gdp,
  population_derivative=b[3]*lambda/pop,
  GDP_one_percent=100*(1.01^b[2]-1),
  population_ratio=(16.75/5.35)^b[3])

Read the mean in expected medals, the derivatives in expected medals per original GDP/population unit, and GDP_one_percent as a percent change. Using β×λ without dividing by GDP would differentiate with respect to log(GDP), not GDP itself.

# Copyable derivative for an unlogged illustrative predictor
b1 <- log(1.5); lambda <- 3
c(local_effect=b1*lambda, exact_one_unit=lambda*(exp(b1)-1))
local_effect exact_one_unit
    1.216395       1.500000

At a fitted mean of 3, the local marginal effect is 1.2164 events per x unit; the exact full-unit mean increase is 1.5. The units and size of the predictor change determine which calculation is appropriate.

Olympic Medals Example

Audit the source data description, read the Poisson output and resolve the medal-prediction discrepancy transparently.

Lecture 3, slides 25–28

What the lecture dataset contains

Source data boundary

The PDF describes 1,610 country-year records, but the original olympics object was not supplied. All full-dataset summaries are labeled lecture-reported. Direct substitution into the displayed coefficients is independently reproducible; refitting those coefficients is not.

Each row is a country-year record. The displayed first eight columns are country, year, gdp, pop, gold, silver, bronze and medaltot. country and year are integer codes, gdp and pop are numeric, and medal columns are integer counts with some NA entries. GDP is described in billions and population in millions. Zero medals is an observed count; NA means missing information and must not be silently replaced by zero.

The displayed model predicts about 0.961 medals for that covariate combination, not a probability of 0.961 of winning.

  1. State the comparison

    At GDP=5.79 billion, compare populations 5.35 million and 16.75 million. Use the coefficients printed on slide 27.

  2. Take natural logs

    ln(5.79)=1.75613229; ln(5.35)=1.67709656; ln(16.75)=2.81839826.

  3. Calculate the first link value

    −1.389530+0.570086×1.75613229+0.207963×1.67709656=−0.0396095343.

  4. Exponentiate the first mean

    exp(−0.0396095343)=0.9611646677.

  5. Change only population

    −1.389530+0.570086×1.75613229+0.207963×2.81839826=0.1977389906; exp(0.1977389906)=1.2186442747.

  6. Compare with the source

    Input populationSlide 28 reportedComputed from slide 27
    5.35 million0.86340.9611646677
    16.75 million1.04951.2186442747

  7. Add a probability if requested

    At the first input, P(Y=0)=exp(−0.9611646677)=0.38244720. P(Y≥2)=1−exp(−λ)(1+λ)=0.24995806. At the second input, P(Y=0)=0.29563069 and P(Y≥2)=0.34410066.

  8. Conclude without guessing the cause

    Both displayed slopes are positive and statistically significant in the reported model. The independently calculated means do not match slide 28. A different fitted model or inputs could explain this, but the PDF supplies insufficient information to determine the cause.

Source discrepancy: slide 28

Retain 0.8634 and 1.0495 as lecture-reported values only. Use 0.9611646677 and 1.2186442747 when asked to substitute into slide 27’s coefficients. Using population 5.353 instead of the rounded 5.35 changes the first mean only slightly (about 0.961277); it does not resolve the discrepancy.

Diagnostics and missing observations

The lecture reports null deviance 23699.8 on 1253 df; residual deviance 8983.6 on 1251 df; 356 observations deleted due to missingness; AIC 10692; and six Fisher scoring iterations. Thus 1610−356=1254 observations enter the model, with 1254−3=1251 residual df. The reported deviance residual five-number summary is −10.0670, −1.7787, −1.0157, −0.3793, 21.6882.

A rough dispersion diagnostic

Dresdfres=8983.61251=7.181135\frac{D_{res}}{df_{res}}=\frac{8983.6}{1251}=7.181135dfres​Dres​​=12518983.6​=7.181135

Dres is residual deviance and dfres its degrees of freedom. This ratio is a rough diagnostic, not a definitive overdispersion test; Pearson residual dispersion is another check.

8983.6≫12518983.6\gg12518983.6≫1251

The large ratio and extreme residuals raise concern about the simple Poisson mean/variance model. Its tiny coefficient p-values rely on the specified Poisson standard errors. Repeated country-years may introduce additional dependence.

For Poisson data, deviance is generally not −2log-likelihood because the saturated log-likelihood is generally not zero. This explains why AIC 10692 is not 8983.6+2×3. Review exposure, dependence, omitted predictors and overdispersion before relying on inference; the PDF alone cannot validate these properties.

Self-check: How many source observations entered the Olympic model?

1254: the null df is 1253 with one intercept, and 1610 original rows minus 356 omitted rows also gives 1254.

Reproduce the displayed-model predictions

# No source CSV is needed to substitute published coefficients.
new <- data.frame(gdp=c(5.79,5.79),pop=c(5.35,16.75))
new$eta <- with(new,-1.389530+0.570086*log(gdp)+0.207963*log(pop))
new$lambda <- exp(new$eta)
new$P0 <- dpois(0,new$lambda)
new$Pge2 <- ppois(1,new$lambda,lower.tail=FALSE)
new
   gdp   pop         eta    lambda        P0     Pge2
1 5.79  5.35 -0.03960953 0.9611647 0.3824472 0.2499581
2 5.79 16.75  0.19773899 1.2186443 0.2956307 0.3441007

The result table explicitly separates link values, expected counts and probabilities. log() is natural logarithm. Positive gdp/pop are required because log(0) is not finite. No new fit is claimed by this block.

with(new,exp(-1.389530+0.570086*log(gdp)+0.207963*log(pop)))

Poisson Regression in R

Fit a count GLM, inspect its diagnostics, and request both expected counts and count probabilities.

Lecture 3, slides 25–28, with a new runnable illustration

A complete reproducible workflow

Use stats::glm(), stats::poisson(), summary(), predict(), dpois() and ppois(); all come with R. ggplot2 is optional for the lecture-style histogram. The miniature countries below are explicitly new data, chosen to make the code independently runnable. They are not the 1,610 source records and must not be used to claim replication of the lecture’s coefficients.

# New illustrative countries, not the lecture's Olympic dataset.
olympics <- data.frame(gdp=c(1,2,5,10,20,50,100,200),
                       pop=c(1,3,2,5,10,20,40,80),
                       medaltot=c(0,1,0,2,3,6,10,18))
poisson_model <- glm(medaltot ~ log(gdp)+log(pop),
                     data=olympics, family=poisson(link="log"))
str(olympics)
summary(olympics$gdp)
summary(olympics$pop)
summary(poisson_model)
new <- data.frame(gdp=20,pop=10)
lambda <- predict(poisson_model,newdata=new,type="response")
c(mean=lambda,P0=dpois(0,lambda),Pge2=ppois(1,lambda,lower.tail=FALSE))
New illustrative fitted coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
