Estimate is a log-mean slope. SE is its model-based uncertainty. z=Estimate/SE tests a coefficient equal to zero asymptotically. These eight illustrative rows have correlated predictors and imprecise separate slopes; the GDP coefficient is slightly negative here, unlike the source fit. The p-values do not demonstrate an independent GDP association in this tiny demonstration. Seven null df and five residual df correspond to eight rows and three fitted coefficients.

Important function arguments

Argument / functionMeaning and choices
medaltot ~ log(gdp)+log(pop)Model the count as a function of two logged predictors. Both must be strictly positive.
family=poisson(link="log")Specify the distribution and link explicitly. The default Poisson dispersion is fixed at 1.
na.actionBy default, R commonly omits rows with missing model variables. Inspect model$na.action and nobs(model); do not assume every imported row was used.
type="response"Returns fitted mean λ. type="link" returns log λ. Neither option directly returns P(Y=y).
offset(log(exposure))An optional model term when counts come from unequal positive exposure durations; its coefficient is fixed at 1. This is a clarifying extension, not a term in the lecture Olympic fit.

Check what the summary does not settle

# New illustrative countries, not the lecture's Olympic dataset.
olympics <- data.frame(gdp=c(1,2,5,10,20,50,100,200),
                       pop=c(1,3,2,5,10,20,40,80),
                       medaltot=c(0,1,0,2,3,6,10,18))
poisson_model <- glm(medaltot ~ log(gdp)+log(pop),
                     data=olympics, family=poisson(link="log"))
c(rows_used=nobs(poisson_model), residual_df=df.residual(poisson_model),
  Pearson_dispersion=sum(residuals(poisson_model,type="pearson")^2)/
                     df.residual(poisson_model))
# Optional lecture-style histogram:
# install.packages("ggplot2") # once if absent
# library(ggplot2)
# ggplot(olympics,aes(x=medaltot))+geom_histogram(binwidth=1)

The Pearson dispersion estimate compares squared standardized residuals with residual degrees of freedom. A ratio far above 1 can signal extra variation, misspecification or dependence; it is not a universal automatic decision rule. A quasi-Poisson mean model can change standard errors, but its usual fit lacks an ordinary likelihood-based AIC. That is an optional diagnostic response, not a replacement silently applied to the lecture model.

Self-check: Does predict(...,type="response")=2.73 mean a probability of 273%?

No. It is an expected count of 2.73. For a probability, use dpois() or ppois() with lambda=2.73.

Copyable fit and interpretation

# New illustrative countries, not the lecture's Olympic dataset.
olympics <- data.frame(gdp=c(1,2,5,10,20,50,100,200),
                       pop=c(1,3,2,5,10,20,40,80),
                       medaltot=c(0,1,0,2,3,6,10,18))
poisson_model <- glm(medaltot ~ log(gdp)+log(pop),
                     data=olympics, family=poisson(link="log"))
print(summary(poisson_model)$coefficients)
lambda <- predict(poisson_model,newdata=data.frame(gdp=20,pop=10),
                  type="response")
print(c(expected=lambda,P0=dpois(0,lambda),
        Pge2=ppois(1,lambda,lower.tail=FALSE)))

For this explicitly illustrative dataset, GDP=20 and population=10 yield fitted expected count 2.7277, zero-count probability 0.0654 and at-least-two probability 0.7563. The GDP slope is poorly estimated and not significant in this small fit. These values and conclusions belong to the illustration; the source Olympic fit is documented separately.

Introduction and Assumptions

Learn why ranks and signs help, and which assumptions nonparametric methods still require.

Lecture 4, slides 3–5

Why nonparametric statistics exists

A student can rank four instructors from strongest to weakest without measuring teaching ability on a meaningful numerical scale. A tea expert can order five brands by taste without claiming that one tastes exactly twice as good as another. These are ordinal observations: their order is meaningful, while arithmetic differences and ratios may not be. Rank methods let us analyze such observations without pretending that the gaps between positions are equal.

Nonparametric procedures also help with numerical observations when a familiar model's distributional assumptions are doubtful. A small collection of highly skewed measurements, for example, may be poorly represented by the normal model behind an exact small-sample t procedure. Replacing measurements with signs or ranks can make the test less dependent on the measurement distribution. The cost is that some information about the original magnitudes is discarded.

In the lecture's terminology, a nonparametric test can compare distributions whose precise form has not been specified. The word does not mean that the population has no parameters or that every possible assumption disappears. A median, a sign probability, or a location shift is still a meaningful target.

What kind of observations do you have?

MeasurementWhat is meaningful?ExampleRelevant method
BinaryTwo categories and their order in timePass/fail in productionRuns test for order
OrdinalOrder, without equal numerical distancesJudge's teaching ranksRank correlation
Quantitative, pairedWithin-person or within-day differencesBlood pressure under two conditionsSign or signed-rank test
Quantitative, independent groupsDifferent observations in each groupStrengths of two paper typesMann–Whitney
Quantitative, several independent groupsGroup membership and pooled orderDefects from three assembly linesKruskal–Wallis

A rank is a position in sorted observations. If values 4, 7, 7, 10 occupy positions 1, 2, 3, 4, the two 7s each receive the midrank (2+3)/2=2.5(2+3)/2=2.5(2+3)/2=2.5. Their assigned ranks still sum to the occupied positions: 2.5+2.5=52.5+2.5=52.5+2.5=5. This is why pooled rank totals remain useful arithmetic checks.

Assumptions to check before calculating

  • Sampling and independence: observations or pairs must be independently selected in a way that supports the intended population inference. Ranking cannot repair selection bias or repeated observations treated as independent.
  • Design: paired measurements stay paired. Two unrelated samples are not paired merely because they have equal lengths.
  • Sign test: under its null, positive and negative nonzero differences are equally likely. It does not require a symmetric distribution of difference magnitudes.
  • Signed-rank test: the paired differences have a symmetric distribution around the hypothesized location. Symmetry makes sign equally likely at each absolute magnitude.
  • Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis: a general null concerns equal distributions. Interpreting a rejection specifically as a location or median difference needs comparable distribution shapes, as in the lecture's location-shift model.
  • Runs test: the original order is essential. Under the conditional null, all arrangements with the observed category totals are equally likely.
  • Correlation: observations come as matched (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​) pairs. Correlation describes association; it does not establish a causal mechanism.
Reading the lecture carefully. Statements such as “no assumptions about the distribution” refer to avoiding a specified normal or other parametric form. They do not remove independence, symmetry where needed, or the conditions for a location interpretation. Equal marginal distributions of two arbitrarily dependent paired variables also do not by themselves guarantee a fair sign; the paired null must justify equal sign probabilities.
Self-check: same subjects, before and after

Use a paired procedure because the two measurements from one subject are related. Analyze within-subject differences. Use the sign test if only the direction is trustworthy; consider signed ranks if magnitudes can be ranked and the difference distribution is plausibly symmetric.

Prepare data before choosing an R function

The functions used in this lecture belong mainly to R's automatically available stats package. Sign and runs tests use the additional DescTools package. Reshaping an advertising example uses reshape. Packages are installed once and loaded in each new session when their unqualified function names are used.

# Install once if needed; internet is required for installation only.
install.packages("DescTools")
install.packages("reshape")

# The guide itself works offline. These commands run in a separate R session.
library(DescTools)

normal <- c(126, 117, 115, 118, 118, 128, 125, 120)
stress <- c(130, 118, 125, 120, 121, 125, 130, 120)
stopifnot(length(normal) == length(stress))
paired <- data.frame(normal, stress)
paired$difference <- paired$normal - paired$stress
str(paired)
paired

c() constructs a vector in the supplied order. data.frame() stores aligned columns. length() counts observations, stopifnot() catches a failed condition, and str() shows column types and sample entries. The object above contains eight paired rows; the last difference is zero. Zero differences and tied absolute differences have distinct roles in the tests.

Choose the function that matches the question

QuestionFunctionImportant setting
Equal sign probabilities in paired differences?DescTools::SignTest(x,y)Order defines x−y
Symmetric paired location shift?stats::wilcox.test(x,y)paired=TRUE
Two independent distributions?stats::wilcox.test(x,y)paired=FALSE
Several independent distributions?stats::kruskal.test(value~group)Group factor identifies samples
Random order in a binary sequence?DescTools::RunsTest(sequence)Keep original order
Monotone or linear association?stats::cor(x,y,method=...)spearman, kendall, or pearson
A function name does not establish that the design is appropriate. The same wilcox.test() function performs two different procedures depending on paired. The browser displays runnable R code and verified reference output; it does not execute an R runtime.

Nonparametric Hypothesis Testing

Connect a null model, a statistic, a tail probability, and a justified decision.

Lecture 4, slides 6,8–9,17–18,26,36,43

From a question to a decision

A hypothesis test asks how surprising an observed statistic would be if a specified null model were true. The statistic compresses the data into a feature relevant to the question: a number of positive differences, a rank sum, an across-group rank separation, or a number of runs. Different questions need different statistics.

  1. Identify the design and target

    Write down what one observation represents, whether samples are related, and what “difference” means. A difference in full distributions is a broader claim than a difference in medians.

  2. State hypotheses before looking at the result

    Use a two-sided alternative for either direction. Use a one-sided alternative only when the scientific question prespecifies a direction. In a paired test with D=X−YD=X-YD=X−Y, “greater” concerns a positive shift of DDD.

  3. Choose a significance level

    α\alphaα controls the planned probability of rejecting a true null. A discrete test may not have a nonrandomized rejection region with exactly the requested probability.

  4. Calculate the statistic under the chosen convention

    Document rank direction, tie handling, zero removal, and which sample comes first. Two valid U conventions can give complementary numerical statistics.

  5. Find a p-value or a critical value

    An exact calculation uses the finite null distribution. An approximation replaces it with a normal or chi-square distribution under suitable conditions. State which method was used.

  6. Decide and interpret

    Compare ppp to the prespecified α\alphaα, or compare the statistic with the matching rejection region. State evidence in the problem's original units and population.

A p-value is a null-model probability

p=PH0(a statistic at least as extreme as observed).p=P_{H_0}(\text{a statistic at least as extreme as observed}).p=PH0​​(a statistic at least as extreme as observed).

PH0P_{H_0}PH0​​ means probability calculated under the null model. “Extreme” depends on the alternative and the exact convention for a discrete two-sided test. It is not the probability that H0H_0H0​ is true.

Factory sign-test substitution: P(M≤2 or M≥8)=112/1024=0.109375P(M\le2\text{ or }M\ge8)=112/1024=0.109375P(M≤2 or M≥8)=112/1024=0.109375. About 10.94% of fair-sign samples of size ten are at least this unbalanced in either direction.

The decision rule

Reject H0 if p≤α;otherwise fail to reject H0.\text{Reject }H_0\text{ if }p\le\alpha;\quad\text{otherwise fail to reject }H_0.Reject H0​ if p≤α;otherwise fail to reject H0​.

Here ppp is calculated from the observations and α\alphaα is chosen in advance. For p=0.109375p=0.109375p=0.109375 and α=0.05\alpha=0.05α=0.05, 0.109375>0.050.109375>0.050.109375>0.05, so fail to reject. This does not prove identical production lines; the evidence is insufficient for this test at this level.

Exact distributions and approximations

For ten independent fair signs there are 210=10242^{10}=1024210=1024 equally likely sign arrangements. For a no-tie two-sample rank test, there are (n1+n2n1)\binom{n_1+n_2}{n_1}(n1​n1​+n2​​) equally likely assignments of group labels to the pooled ranks. A signed-rank exact test assigns signs to observed absolute ranks. A runs exact test conditions on the two category totals and counts arrangements in their original sequence positions.

Small-sample tables typically assume no ties. Averaging tied ranks is the correct data preparation, but it does not make the original no-tie reference distribution valid. A conditional exact calculation can account for the observed ties. A tie-corrected large-sample approximation is another method, with potentially different p-values.

A continuity correction moves a discrete statistic's boundary by roughly half a unit before using a continuous normal curve. For a two-sided normal approximation, move toward the null mean: Zcc=sign⁡(S−μ)max⁡(∣S−μ∣−0.5,0)/σZ_{cc}=\operatorname{sign}(S-\mu)\max(|S-\mu|-0.5,0)/\sigmaZcc​=sign(S−μ)max(∣S−μ∣−0.5,0)/σ. Here SSS is the directional statistic, μ\muμ its null mean, and σ\sigmaσ its null standard deviation. Do not add another correction to an exact p-value.

A statistical decision concerns evidence, not certainty or practical importance. A small p-value does not measure effect size; a large p-value does not establish equivalence. Choosing a one-sided alternative after seeing the direction changes the procedure and its error control.

Read and compute tail probabilities in R

Distribution functions in stats use a prefix: d for an individual probability or density, p for a cumulative probability, and q for a quantile. For a discrete random variable, an upper tail including the observation requires care.

# Exact binomial signs under H0
n <- 10
m <- 2
dbinom(m, size = n, prob = 0.5)  # P(M = 2)
pbinom(m, size = n, prob = 0.5)  # P(M <= 2)
pbinom(7, size = n, prob = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE) # P(M >= 8)
2 * pbinom(min(m, n - m), size = n, prob = 0.5)

# Upper-tail chi-square critical value and p-value
qchisq(0.05, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
pchisq(6.097, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-sided standard normal p-value
z <- -1.684024198
2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
# Expected numerical results, in command order
0.0439453125
0.0546875
0.0546875
0.109375
5.991464547
0.04743002
0.09217699

size is the number of Bernoulli trials and prob the null success probability. lower.tail=FALSE requests P(M>q)P(M>q)P(M>q), not P(M≥q)P(M\ge q)P(M≥q); use q=7q=7q=7 to include 8. For a continuous chi-square variable the boundary has probability zero. df gives degrees of freedom. abs() and pnorm() give both normal tails as 2Φ(−∣z∣)2\Phi(-|z|)2Φ(−∣z∣).

What an htest result means

Most tests return an htest object with a statistic, a p-value, the method name, and the alternative. A printed method containing “continuity correction” identifies an approximation. “Exact” identifies an exact null calculation under that function's assumptions. A displayed statistic called V or W may differ from the lecture's T or U by a complement or a subtraction; reconcile definitions before comparing numbers.

a <- c(163, 198, 160, 193, 182, 202, 173, 177, 192, 180)
b <- c(190, 179, 176, 178, 184, 210, 194, 203, 204, 181)
result <- binom.test(sum(a > b), length(a), p = 0.5)
result$statistic
result$p.value
result$alternative
alpha <- 0.05
if (result$p.value <= alpha) "Reject H0" else "Fail to reject H0"

This runnable example has no ties. With ties, create the nonzero-difference vector first and use its length. The final expression returns “Fail to reject H0” at 5%.

Sign Test for Matched Pairs

Use only the direction of paired differences and calculate the exact binomial evidence.

Lecture 4, slides 7–14

The question the sign test answers

The sign test asks whether a paired difference tends to be positive or negative. It ignores the size of a change. This is useful when observations are matched but a magnitude-based model is difficult to justify: two production lines observed on the same days, or ratings of two alternatives from the same respondent. Day-to-day conditions may influence both lines, so the day is the pairing unit.

Define Di=Xi−YiD_i=X_i-Y_iDi​=Xi​−Yi​. Under the continuous median-zero null, a positive difference has probability p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2. The hypotheses are H0:p=1/2H_0:p=1/2H0​:p=1/2, with Ha:p>1/2H_a:p>1/2Ha​:p>1/2, p<1/2p<1/2p<1/2, or p≠1/2p\ne1/2p=1/2. In words: positive and negative differences are equally likely, versus a specified directional imbalance or either imbalance. Independent pairs are essential; the two observations within a pair may be dependent.

Calculate each paired difference

Di=Xi−Yi.D_i=X_i-Y_i.Di​=Xi​−Yi​.

iii labels the pair, XiX_iXi​ is the first measurement, and YiY_iYi​ the second. Factory day 1: D1=163−190=−27D_1=163-190=-27D1​=163−190=−27. The negative sign means line A produced fewer defects than B that day. The sign defines the evidence direction; −27 and −1 each contribute one negative sign.

Count positive differences

M=∑i=1nI(Di>0),M∣H0∼Binomial⁡(n,1/2).M=\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(D_i>0),\qquad M\mid H_0\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/2).M=i=1∑n​I(Di​>0),M∣H0​∼Binomial(n,1/2).

I(⋅)I(\cdot)I(⋅) is 1 when its condition is true and 0 otherwise; nnn is the number of nonzero valid differences. In the factory example M=0+1+0+1+0+0+0+0+0+0=2M=0+1+0+1+0+0+0+0+0+0=2M=0+1+0+1+0+0+0+0+0+0=2, and n=10n=10n=10. Under the null the expected number of positives is np=10(0.5)=5np=10(0.5)=5np=10(0.5)=5; two is below this expectation.

An individual binomial probability

P(M=m)=(nm)pm(1−p)n−m.P(M=m)=\binom{n}{m}p^m(1-p)^{n-m}.P(M=m)=(mn​)pm(1−p)n−m.

mmm is a possible count and (nm)\binom{n}{m}(mn​) counts which pairs have positive signs. With n=10,p=0.5,m=2n=10,p=0.5,m=2n=10,p=0.5,m=2, P(M=2)=45(0.5)10=45/1024=0.0439453125P(M=2)=45(0.5)^{10}=45/1024=0.0439453125P(M=2)=45(0.5)10=45/1024=0.0439453125. This is only the probability of exactly two positives, not the full p-value.

Cumulative and two-sided evidence

P(M≤2)=∑j=02(10j)2−10=1+10+451024=0.0546875.P(M\le2)=\sum_{j=0}^{2}\binom{10}{j}2^{-10}=\frac{1+10+45}{1024}=0.0546875.P(M≤2)=j=0∑2​(j10​)2−10=10241+10+45​=0.0546875.

jjj enumerates counts at least as low as the observed count. Symmetry of the fair-sign distribution gives ptwo=P(M≤2)+P(M≥8)=2(0.0546875)=0.109375.p_{two}=P(M\le2)+P(M\ge8)=2(0.0546875)=0.109375.ptwo​=P(M≤2)+P(M≥8)=2(0.0546875)=0.109375. These are the two directions of imbalance. In general the two-sided fair-sign value is min⁡[1,2P{M≤min⁡(m,n−m)}]\min[1,2P\{M\le\min(m,n-m)\}]min[1,2P{M≤min(m,n−m)}].

Worked example: production-line defects

  1. Original problem and dataset

    Compare daily defect counts from lines A and B over ten matched days. Is either line systematically higher?

    DayABA−BSign
    1163190−27−
    219817919+
    3160176−16−
    419317815+
    5182184−2−
    6202210−8−
    7173194−21−
    8177203−26−
    9192204−12−
    10180181−1−

  2. Design, assumptions, and hypotheses

    Each day is one pair; assume independently representative days. Set D=A−BD=A-BD=A−B, H0:P(D>0)=0.5H_0:P(D>0)=0.5H0​:P(D>0)=0.5, and Ha:P(D>0)≠0.5H_a:P(D>0)\ne0.5Ha​:P(D>0)=0.5. For a conventional comparison, choose α=0.05\alpha=0.05α=0.05 in advance.

  3. Prepare signs and calculate the statistic

    There are no zero differences. Days 2 and 4 are positive; the other eight are negative. Thus m=2,n=10m=2,n=10m=2,n=10. The exact null model is Binomial(10,0.5).

  4. Calculate exact tails

    The lower-tail numerator is (100)+(101)+(102)=1+10+45=56\binom{10}{0}+\binom{10}{1}+\binom{10}{2}=1+10+45=56(010​)+(110​)+(210​)=1+10+45=56. Divide by 210=10242^{10}=1024210=1024, then include the symmetric upper tail: p=112/1024=0.109375p=112/1024=0.109375p=112/1024=0.109375.

  5. Make a conventional decision

    0.109375>0.050.109375>0.050.109375>0.05; fail to reject. The same p-value exceeds 0.10, so it also fails to reject at a conventional 10% level.

  6. Interpret in context

    A produced fewer defects on eight of ten sampled days, but this sample does not provide enough sign-test evidence at 5% to conclude that one line has a systematically higher paired defect distribution. This is not proof of equal quality.

The lecture's rejection region and its chosen size

Slides 11–13 construct a rejection region by adding equally extreme pairs of counts. Its actual null rejection probability increases in discrete jumps:

Rejection regionExact numerator /1024Actual αReject m=2?
{0,10}20.001953125No
{0,1,9,10}2(1+10)=220.021484375No
{0,1,2,8,9,10}2(1+10+45)=1120.109375Yes
Preserved source decision, with its condition. The lecture explicitly accepts an actual rejection probability of about 0.109 and therefore rejects for m=2. That decision is consistent with its chosen region. It is not a rejection at α=0.05 or α=0.10. At a requested maximum level of 0.05, the largest symmetric nonrandomized region here has actual size 0.021484375. The p-value and the requested significance level must remain distinct.

Zero differences and the median interpretation

Delete pairs with Di=0D_i=0Di​=0 for the lecture's sign procedure, then reduce nnn. A tie contributes neither a positive nor a negative sign. If one zero were added to the example, ten nonzero signs would remain; using eleven trials would be wrong. When a population has a substantial mass at zero, distinguish the equal probability of positive and negative nonzero differences from claims about an unconditional median.

The sample median difference is −10: sort the differences as −27, −26, −21, −16, −12, −8, −2, −1, 15, 19, then average the middle pair, (−12−8)/2=−10(-12-8)/2=-10(−12−8)/2=−10. A distribution-free order-statistic interval is [−26,15]. Its attainable coverage is 1−2P{Bin⁡(10,0.5)≤1}=0.9785156251-2P\{\operatorname{Bin}(10,0.5)\le1\}=0.9785156251−2P{Bin(10,0.5)≤1}=0.978515625, explaining the 97.9% confidence interval displayed by R despite a nominal 95% request.

Self-check: reverse A and B

The positive count becomes 8 instead of 2. The two-sided p-value stays 0.109375. A directional alternative must reverse too: “A has fewer” using A−B is a lower-tail test, while the same scientific statement using B−A is an upper-tail test.

Reproduce the exact sign test in R

DescTools::SignTest() performs the paired sign test and reports a median difference and an order-statistic confidence interval. Install DescTools once with install.packages("DescTools"). Using the namespace prefix makes the required package explicit without a separate library() call.

a <- c(163, 198, 160, 193, 182, 202, 173, 177, 192, 180)
b <- c(190, 179, 176, 178, 184, 210, 194, 203, 204, 181)
d <- a - b
data.frame(day = seq_along(a), a, b, difference = d, positive = d > 0)
table(d > 0)
DescTools::SignTest(x = a, y = b, mu = 0,
                    alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
# Lecture output, verified with R 4.5 / DescTools
Dependent-samples Sign-Test
S = 2, number of differences = 10, p-value = 0.1094
alternative hypothesis: true median difference is not equal to 0
97.9 percent confidence interval:
 -26  15
sample estimates:
median of the differences
 -10

Read the output: S is the number of positive differences, identical to lecture M. “Number of differences” counts valid nonzero differences. The p-value rounds 0.109375. The interval contains zero, and its exact attainable coverage is 97.8516%, printed 97.9%. The estimate −10 is the sample median of A−B; it does not replace the sign statistic.

General syntax and arguments

DescTools::SignTest(x, y = NULL, mu = 0,
                    alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
  • x: a numeric vector; with y, the first measurement in each pair.
  • y: an optional numeric vector of matched second measurements. Omit it to test one vector against mu.
  • mu: hypothesized median difference, zero by default. For “the median increase equals 5,” set the difference orientation and mu=5.
  • alternative: "two.sided", "less", or "greater", referring to x−y relative to mu. A less test here asks whether A tends lower than B.
  • conf.level: requested confidence level. Discrete order statistics may produce a different attainable exact coverage, which the output labels.

Connect the function to the binomial calculation

# Transparent manual reproduction, including zeros and missing pairs
ok <- complete.cases(a, b)
d <- a[ok] - b[ok]
d <- d[d != 0]
n <- length(d)
m <- sum(d > 0)

dbinom(0, n, 0.5) + dbinom(n, n, 0.5)
# 0.001953125
sum(dbinom(c(0, 1, 9, 10), n, 0.5))
# 0.021484375
sum(dbinom(c(0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10), n, 0.5))
# 0.109375

p.lower <- pbinom(m, size = n, prob = 0.5)
p.two <- min(1, 2 * pbinom(min(m, n - m), n, 0.5))
binom.test(m, n, p = 0.5, alternative = "two.sided")
DescTools::SignTest(a, b, alternative = "less")

dbinom() gives a single count's probability; summing it builds the rejection region. pbinom() sums a cumulative tail. binom.test(), in stats, supplies the exact fair-sign p-value; its confidence interval concerns a binomial probability, so it is not the same interval as SignTest's median-difference interval. The one-sided less p-value is 0.0546875; it also exceeds 0.05.

Copyable exam example

# Objects a and b are the complete vectors defined above.
fit <- DescTools::SignTest(a, b, alternative = "two.sided")
fit$p.value
# 0.109375

There are two positive differences among ten nonzero pairs. The exact two-sided p-value is 0.109375, so at α=0.05 fail to reject a median-zero paired difference. The lecture instead rejects under its expressly accepted region of actual size 0.109375; state that convention if reproducing its decision.

Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test

Combine paired change directions with their ranked magnitudes, and reconcile lecture T with R V.

Lecture 4, slides 15–22

Why use signed ranks?

The sign test treats a change of 1 and a change of 18 equally. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test adds information about relative magnitudes while avoiding a specified normal distribution. Rank the absolute paired differences, then ask whether the large ranks tend to have the same sign. It is a paired procedure: each subject or experimental unit supplies both measurements.

The lecture describes a null of no location difference between paired populations. A precise working model is that independent paired differences Di=Xi−YiD_i=X_i-Y_iDi​=Xi​−Yi​ have a distribution symmetric around a location θ\thetaθ. Test H0:θ=0H_0:\theta=0H0​:θ=0, versus θ≠0\theta\ne0θ=0, θ>0\theta>0θ>0, or θ<0\theta<0θ<0. Under symmetry, the center is also the median. Without symmetry this is not a general distribution-free test of an arbitrary population median.

Prepare differences and ranks

  1. Choose and retain the difference orientation

    Use Di=Xi−YiD_i=X_i-Y_iDi​=Xi​−Yi​. Subtract only measurements from the same pair. A positive difference means X is higher.

  2. Remove zero differences

    A zero has no positive or negative sign. Remove it before ranking and let nnn count remaining nonzero pairs. This is the lecture's convention, also used in the R examples here.

  3. Rank the absolute differences together

    Sort ∣Di∣|D_i|∣Di​∣ from smallest to largest, assigning ranks 1 through n. Equal absolute magnitudes receive their average occupied rank, whether their signs agree or differ.

  4. Restore signs and sum ranks

    Add the ranks belonging to positive differences and separately those belonging to negative differences. Check that their sum is n(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2.

Positive and negative rank sums

T+=∑Di>0ri,T−=∑Di<0ri,T++T−=n(n+1)2.T^+=\sum_{D_i>0}r_i,\quad T^-=\sum_{D_i<0}r_i,\quad T^++T^-=\frac{n(n+1)}2.T+=Di​>0∑​ri​,T−=Di​<0∑​ri​,T++T−=2n(n+1)​.

rir_iri​ is the rank of ∣Di∣|D_i|∣Di​∣ after zero removal; nnn is the nonzero sample size. Exam substitution: T+=5.5+4+1=10.5T^+=5.5+4+1=10.5T+=5.5+4+1=10.5, T−=5.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.5T^-=5.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.5T−=5.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.5. The check is 10.5+44.5=55=10(11)/210.5+44.5=55=10(11)/210.5+44.5=55=10(11)/2. Negative differences carry most of the rank mass.

The lecture's two-sided statistic

T=min⁡(T+,T−).T=\min(T^+,T^-).T=min(T+,T−).

For the exams, T=min⁡(10.5,44.5)=10.5T=\min(10.5,44.5)=10.5T=min(10.5,44.5)=10.5. A small minimum signals an imbalance in either direction. With a prespecified X-higher alternative, the lecture instead uses a small T−T^-T−; with X-lower it uses a small T+T^+T+. R always reports the directional positive sum V for a paired call, rather than automatically reporting the minimum.

Worked example: two midterms

  1. Original dataset

    Ten students took two midterms. These are the same students, so use within-student differences X−Y.

    StudentXYD|D|RankContribution
    17885−775.5T−
    28095−15159T−
    36770−332.5T−
    49184775.5T+
    58579664T+
    67694−181810T−
    79695111T+
    85968−997T−
    97487−13138T−
    108891−332.5T−

  2. State assumptions and hypotheses

    Assume independent student pairs and a symmetric difference distribution. Test a zero paired location shift against either direction at α=0.05\alpha=0.05α=0.05. No zero differences are present.

  3. Explain the ties

    The two absolute 3s occupy ranks 2 and 3, so each gets 2.5. The two absolute 7s occupy ranks 5 and 6, so each gets 5.5. Do not rank signed differences directly.

  4. Add signed ranks

    Positive ranks: 5.5+4+1=10.55.5+4+1=10.55.5+4+1=10.5. Negative ranks: 5.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.55.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.55.5+9+2.5+10+7+8+2.5=44.5. Thus T=10.5T=10.5T=10.5, while R's V is also 10.5 in this example because the positive sum happens to be the smaller sum.

  5. Find a matching p-value

    The lecture uses a tie-corrected normal approximation with continuity correction. The next formula cards calculate mean, variance, standard deviation, and Z separately. They give Z=−1.6840242Z=-1.6840242Z=−1.6840242 and two-sided p=0.09217699p=0.09217699p=0.09217699.

  6. Decide and interpret

    Because 0.09218>0.050.09218>0.050.09218>0.05, fail to reject a zero symmetric paired location shift. The negative rank sum suggests Y tends higher, but the two-sided evidence is insufficient at 5%. This does not establish that every student's grades or both full marginal distributions are identical.

Normal approximation: every intermediate quantity

Expected directional rank sum

μT+=E(T+)=n(n+1)4.\mu_{T^+}=E(T^+)=\frac{n(n+1)}4.μT+​=E(T+)=4n(n+1)​.

Each rank has probability one half of receiving a positive sign. For n=10, μT+=10(11)/4=27.5\mu_{T^+}=10(11)/4=27.5μT+​=10(11)/4=27.5, half the total rank sum 55. The same expectation holds for T−T^-T−. It is not the mean of min⁡(T+,T−)\min(T^+,T^-)min(T+,T−).

Null variance, with and without ties

σT+2=n(n+1)(2n+1)24−∑j(tj3−tj)48=14∑iri2.\sigma^2_{T^+}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{24}-\frac{\sum_j(t_j^3-t_j)}{48}=\frac14\sum_i r_i^2.σT+2​=24n(n+1)(2n+1)​−48∑j​(tj3​−tj​)​=41​i∑​ri2​.

tjt_jtj​ is the size of absolute-rank tie group j; the sum is zero when there are no ties. Variance measures squared spread of the null statistic, not standard deviation. Exams: 10(11)(21)/24=96.2510(11)(21)/24=96.2510(11)(21)/24=96.25, then subtract [(23−2)+(23−2)]/48=0.25[(2^3-2)+(2^3-2)]/48=0.25[(23−2)+(23−2)]/48=0.25. The corrected variance is 969696.

Standard deviation of the statistic

σT+=σT+2=96=9.797958971.\sigma_{T^+}=\sqrt{\sigma^2_{T^+}}=\sqrt{96}=9.797958971.σT+​=σT+2​​=96​=9.797958971.

This is the null sampling standard deviation of a rank sum, sometimes loosely called its standard error. It is not the standard deviation of the original exam marks and is not 96.

Standardize and apply a continuity correction

Z=T+−μT+σT+,Zcc=10.5−27.5+0.596=−1.684024198.Z=\frac{T^+-\mu_{T^+}}{\sigma_{T^+}},\qquad Z_{cc}=\frac{10.5-27.5+0.5}{\sqrt{96}}=-1.684024198.Z=σT+​T+−μT+​​,Zcc​=96​10.5−27.5+0.5​=−1.684024198.

The uncorrected numerator is −17. A half-unit move toward zero gives −16.5 before division. The statistic lies about 1.68 null standard deviations below its expectation. For a positive deviation the correction subtracts 0.5 instead.

Convert Z to evidence

ptwo=2Φ(−∣Zcc∣)=2Φ(−1.684024198)=0.0921769923.p_{two}=2\Phi(-|Z_{cc}|)=2\Phi(-1.684024198)=0.0921769923.ptwo​=2Φ(−∣Zcc​∣)=2Φ(−1.684024198)=0.0921769923.

Φ\PhiΦ is the standard normal cumulative distribution. For a prespecified lower-tail alternative use Φ(Z)\Phi(Z)Φ(Z); for an upper-tail alternative use 1−Φ(Z)1-\Phi(Z)1−Φ(Z). At two-sided 5%, the normal critical values are approximately ±1.96, so this statistic remains outside the rejection tails.

Exact tables versus approximate calculations

With independent symmetric nonzero differences, each allocation of signs to the observed absolute ranks has probability 2−n2^{-n}2−n. With no ties, these are subset sums of 1 through n. A lower-tail critical table records the largest c whose cumulative probability is no greater than a chosen tail size. A two-sided test based on the minimum uses a one-tail probability α/2\alpha/2α/2.

The lecture refers to textbook Table 9 but does not reproduce its entries. The following table is independently generated from the exact no-tie sign distribution. “None” means even the most extreme nonrandomized outcome is too probable to attain that level. Use the reduced n after dropping zeros.

Worked example: blood pressure under stress

  1. Data and direction

    Eight subjects perform a puzzle in normal and stressful conditions. Test whether stress tends to raise blood pressure. Set D=Normal−Stress, so the one-sided alternative is a negative location shift.

    SubjectNormalStressDRank of |D|
    1126130−45
    2117118−11
    3115125−107
    4118120−22
    5118121−33.5
    612812533.5
    7125130−56
    81201200Removed

  2. Assumptions and hypotheses

    Assume independent subjects and symmetric nonzero difference distribution. Test H0:θ=0H_0:\theta=0H0​:θ=0 against Ha:θ<0H_a:\theta<0Ha​:θ<0, at α=.05. Drop the last zero, giving n=7.

  3. Rank and sum

    The absolute 3s share ranks 3 and 4, giving 3.5 each. T+=3.5T^+=3.5T+=3.5, T−=5+1+7+2+3.5+6=24.5T^-=5+1+7+2+3.5+6=24.5T−=5+1+7+2+3.5+6=24.5. Their total is 28=7(8)/228=7(8)/228=7(8)/2. A small positive sum favors Normal<Stress.

  4. Exact conditional calculation

    There are 27=1282^7=12827=128 equally likely sign assignments to ranks 1,2,3.5,3.5,5,6,7. Positive sums at most 3.5 arise from the empty subset; {1}; {2}; {1,2}; and either of the two single 3.5s. Six assignments give p=6/128=0.046875p=6/128=0.046875p=6/128=0.046875.

  5. Approximation for comparison

    μ=7(8)/4=14\mu=7(8)/4=14μ=7(8)/4=14; σ2=7(8)(15)/24−(23−2)/48=35−0.125=34.875\sigma^2=7(8)(15)/24-(2^3-2)/48=35-0.125=34.875σ2=7(8)(15)/24−(23−2)/48=35−0.125=34.875; σ=5.905505906\sigma=5.905505906σ=5.905505906. Zcc=(3.5−14+0.5)/5.905505906=−1.693335027Z_{cc}=(3.5-14+0.5)/5.905505906=-1.693335027Zcc​=(3.5−14+0.5)/5.905505906=−1.693335027, giving lower-tail p=0.04519586.

  6. Decision and interpretation

    Both identified methods give p<.05. Reject a zero symmetric paired location in favor of higher stress-condition pressure. This evidence concerns these paired conditions and the target population; it does not measure a universal causal effect without considering the experimental design.

Do not use the no-tie n=7 critical value 3 by rounding the observed tied sum 3.5. Ties change the exact distribution. Also distinguish the screenshot's expected directional sum from the mean of the minimum: its n=7, T+=22 and T−=6 give μ=14 and SD=√35 for either directional sum. The minimum is selected for tail logic, not assigned those same moments.
Self-check: do +7 and −7 get different ranks?

No. Their absolute magnitudes tie, so each receives the same midrank. Their ranks enter different sign sums. For the exam data they each get 5.5, one in T+ and one in T−.

Use stats::wilcox.test for paired differences

The stats package is part of R; no installation or library command is needed. A paired call performs a signed-rank test, not the independent rank-sum test.

wilcox.test(x, y = NULL, paired = FALSE, mu = 0,
            alternative = "two.sided", exact = NULL,
            correct = TRUE, conf.int = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95)
  • x,y: aligned numeric vectors for the same pairs. With only x, test one vector of differences against mu.
  • paired=TRUE: form x−y. Leaving FALSE changes the statistical procedure.
  • mu=0: the hypothesized symmetric location. Subtracting mu precedes sign/rank construction.
  • alternative: two.sided, less, or greater for x−y relative to mu. Swapping x and y reverses a directional test.
  • exact: request exact inference or a normal approximation. To reproduce the lecture's tied-data output, explicitly use exact=FALSE.
  • correct=TRUE: apply a half-unit continuity correction in the normal approximation. It is irrelevant for an exact test.
  • conf.int,conf.level: optionally request a location interval and its confidence level. The estimate is a pseudomedian; under symmetry it agrees with the population center, not necessarily the observed sample median.
The lecture's output and the verified R 4.5 behavior approximate when ties or zeros prevent its default no-tie exact algorithm. Newer R development versions support additional conditional exact calculations. Explicitly selecting exact=FALSE and correct=TRUE makes the lecture comparison reproducible across such default changes.

Complete runnable midterm example

x <- c(78, 80, 67, 91, 85, 76, 96, 59, 74, 88)
y <- c(85, 95, 70, 84, 79, 94, 95, 68, 87, 91)
d <- x - y
r <- rank(abs(d), ties.method = "average")
data.frame(x, y, difference = d, rank = r)
t.plus <- sum(r[d > 0])
t.minus <- sum(r[d < 0])
c(T.plus = t.plus, T.minus = t.minus, T = min(t.plus, t.minus))
wilcox.test(x, y, paired = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided",
            exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
T.plus T.minus      T
  10.5    44.5   10.5

Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction
V = 10.5, p-value = 0.09218
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

V is T+T^+T+, the positive rank sum. It happens to equal the lecture minimum here; reversing the inputs would report V=44.5 with the same two-sided p-value. The method line explains why the output is approximate. The p-value is 0.09218 after rounding, so fail to reject at .05.

Complete runnable blood-pressure example

normal <- c(126, 117, 115, 118, 118, 128, 125, 120)
stress <- c(130, 118, 125, 120, 121, 125, 130, 120)
d <- normal - stress
d <- d[d != 0]                    # seven nonzero differences
r <- rank(abs(d))
c(T.plus = sum(r[d > 0]), T.minus = sum(r[d < 0]))
wilcox.test(normal, stress, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less",
            exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
T.plus T.minus
   3.5    24.5

Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction
V = 3.5, p-value = 0.0452
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is less than 0

Because the first vector is Normal, “less” is the stress-higher question. The small positive sum supports a negative Normal−Stress location. Setting alternative="two.sided" instead gives p≈0.09039; a different scientific question produces a different tail probability.

Optional exact conditional calculation with ties

This small-sample teaching code enumerates the observed ranks' sign assignments. It is not an efficient general algorithm for large n.

# Continue with the seven nonzero blood-pressure differences above.
bits <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(0:1), length(r))))
possible.positive.sums <- drop(bits %*% r)
observed <- sum(r[d > 0])
mean(possible.positive.sums <= observed)
# 0.046875 = 6/128

# Normal calculation, shown separately
mu <- sum(r) / 2
variance <- sum(r^2) / 4
z <- (observed - mu + 0.5) / sqrt(variance)
pnorm(z)
# 0.04519586

rank() averages ties by default; expand.grid() builds all sign masks; matrix multiplication sums the ranks marked positive; mean(condition) is the fraction of equally likely masks in the tail. This directly connects the 6/128 manual calculation to executable R.

Copyable exam interpretation

fit <- wilcox.test(normal, stress, paired = TRUE,
                   alternative = "less", exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
fit$statistic
fit$p.value

The paired signed-rank test gives V=3.5 and an approximate one-sided p-value of 0.04520. Assuming independent subjects and symmetric paired differences, reject a zero location shift at 5% in favor of higher blood pressure under stress. An independently enumerated conditional exact p-value is 0.046875 and supports the same decision.

Mann–Whitney U Test

Compare independent samples using pair counts or pooled ranks, with explicit U and W conventions.

Lecture 4, slides 23–32

Two independent samples

Mann–Whitney compares the ordering of observations from two independent groups. For example, ten randomly selected standard-paper pieces and ten different treated-paper pieces form independent samples. They are not matched pairs. The method uses all cross-group comparisons or, equivalently, pooled ranks. It avoids a specified normal distribution.

The lecture's null is H0:FX=FYH_0:F_X=F_YH0​:FX​=FY​, equal population distributions. A two-sided alternative describes a difference, while one-sided alternatives describe X shifted to the right or left of Y. To interpret this specifically as a location or median comparison, assume the distributions have the same shape and differ only by a shift. With different shapes a rank result is not automatically a median result. The probability-of-superiority quantity P(X>Y)+12P(X=Y)P(X>Y)+\tfrac12P(X=Y)P(X>Y)+21​P(X=Y) helps interpret pairwise ordering, but a null for that probability alone is weaker than full distributional equality.

Lecture page 24: direct pair counting

Sample I: 11, 15, 19, 25. Sample II: 21, 24, 28, 29. Sort all eight observations together:

Value1115192124252829
SampleIIIIIIIIIIII
Pooled rank12345678

The lecture's U counts X before Y

UL=∑i=1n1∑j=1n2[I(xi<yj)+12I(xi=yj)].U_L=\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2}\left[I(x_i<y_j)+\frac12I(x_i=y_j)\right].UL​=i=1∑n1​​j=1∑n2​​[I(xi​<yj​)+21​I(xi​=yj​)].

n1,n2n_1,n_2n1​,n2​ are sample sizes; III is an indicator. Each cross-sample pair contributes 1 for x<y, 0 for x>y, or half for a tie. There are 4×4=164\times4=164×4=16 comparisons. For y=21 there are 3 preceding x values; y=24 also has 3; y=28 and 29 each have 4. Thus UL=3+3+4+4=14U_L=3+3+4+4=14UL​=3+3+4+4=14. A large lecture U means X tends smaller than Y.

Lecture page 25: the equivalent rank-sum method

Raw pooled rank sum

WX=∑i=1n1R(xi).W_X=\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}R(x_i).WX​=i=1∑n1​​R(xi​).

R(xi)R(x_i)R(xi​) is the rank of an X observation among both samples. Here WX=1+2+3+6=12W_X=1+2+3+6=12WX​=1+2+3+6=12. This is the raw rank sum called W on lecture page 25; R's printed W is adjusted and is a different numerical quantity.

Convert the raw rank sum to the lecture U

UL=n1n2+n1(n1+1)2−WX.U_L=n_1n_2+\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}2-W_X.UL​=n1​n2​+2n1​(n1​+1)​−WX​.

The second term is the minimum possible rank sum for the first sample. Substitute: UL=4(4)+4(5)/2−12=16+10−12=14U_L=4(4)+4(5)/2-12=16+10-12=14UL​=4(4)+4(5)/2−12=16+10−12=14, matching direct counting. As X ranks get larger, its raw rank sum rises and this U falls.

The complementary U reported by R as W

UR=WX−n1(n1+1)2=n1n2−UL.U_R=W_X-\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}2=n_1n_2-U_L.UR​=WX​−2n1​(n1​+1)​=n1​n2​−UL​.

Here UR=12−10=2U_R=12-10=2UR​=12−10=2, while UL=14U_L=14UL​=14, and 2+14=162+14=162+14=16. URU_RUR​ counts X>Y plus half ties, so it rises when X tends larger. Many references call these U₁ and U₂, with labels sometimes reversed. Define the direction, not just the subscript.

A two-sided small-tail statistic

Umin=min⁡(UL,UR)=min⁡(14,2)=2.U_{min}=\min(U_L,U_R)=\min(14,2)=2.Umin​=min(UL​,UR​)=min(14,2)=2.

The minimum locates the distance into either tail. It does not preserve the direction of the shift. For a one-sided question, retain the corresponding directional statistic and the correct tail.

Exact distribution, tables, and rejection tails

Without ties, U takes integer values from 0 to n1n2n_1n_2n1​n2​. Under equal continuous distributions its distribution is symmetric around n1n2/2n_1n_2/2n1​n2​/2. In the lecture convention, X shifted right gives small U; X shifted left gives large U.

Symmetric tail probabilities

P(U≤c)=P(U≥n1n2−c).P(U\le c)=P(U\ge n_1n_2-c).P(U≤c)=P(U≥n1​n2​−c).

ccc is a lower-tail cutoff. For n₁=n₂=4 and c=2, P(U≤2)=P(U≥14)=4/70=0.0571428571P(U\le2)=P(U\ge14)=4/70=0.0571428571P(U≤2)=P(U≥14)=4/70=0.0571428571. Consequently the two-sided probability for the observed U=14 is 8/70=0.11428571438/70=0.11428571438/70=0.1142857143. The denominator is (84)=70\binom84=70(48​)=70, the number of equally likely group allocations.

Choose critical values with matching tails

Two-sided: reject if U≤c or U≥n1n2−c,P(U≤c)≤α/2.\text{Two-sided: reject if }U\le c\text{ or }U\ge n_1n_2-c,\quad P(U\le c)\le\alpha/2.Two-sided: reject if U≤c or U≥n1​n2​−c,P(U≤c)≤α/2.

At α=.05 and n₁=n₂=4, choose c=0 because its lower-tail probability is 1/70=.0142857; c=1 would give 2/70=.0285714, exceeding .025. Observed U=14 is not at least 16, so do not reject. For a one-sided .05 test choose c=1, with the tail determined by the alternative. Discreteness can make the actual size less than the requested level.

Large-sample approximation: mean, variance, SD, and Z

Lecture page 32 suggests a normal approximation when both sample sizes exceed ten. This is a rule of thumb; balance, ties, and tail extremity also matter. For small samples prefer a suitable exact distribution. The following cards use the kraft-paper data so that the intermediate quantities have a concrete meaning.

Expected U under equal ordering

μU=E(U)=n1n22.\mu_U=E(U)=\frac{n_1n_2}{2}.μU​=E(U)=2n1​n2​​.

Each of the n₁n₂ cross-group comparisons contributes an expected half under the null. Ten paper pieces in each group give μU=10(10)/2=50\mu_U=10(10)/2=50μU​=10(10)/2=50. Both complementary U conventions have this same null mean.

Null variance without ties

σU2=n1n2(n1+n2+1)12.\sigma_U^2=\frac{n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)}{12}.σU2​=12n1​n2​(n1​+n2​+1)​.

For n₁=n₂=10, σU2=100(21)/12=175\sigma_U^2=100(21)/12=175σU2​=100(21)/12=175. This is squared spread of the rank statistic under the null, not variability of paper strengths. The next correction is needed because the paper sample has ties.

Tie-corrected null variance

σU2=n1n212[N+1−∑j(tj3−tj)N(N−1)],N=n1+n2.\sigma_U^2=\frac{n_1n_2}{12}\left[N+1-\frac{\sum_j(t_j^3-t_j)}{N(N-1)}\right],\quad N=n_1+n_2.σU2​=12n1​n2​​[N+1−N(N−1)∑j​(tj3​−tj​)​],N=n1​+n2​.

tjt_jtj​ is a tied group size in the pooled measurements. Two observations equal 1.29 and two equal 1.37, so the tie sum is 6+6=126+6=126+6=12. Substitution gives 10012[21−12/(20⋅19)]=174.7368421053\frac{100}{12}[21-12/(20\cdot19)]=174.736842105312100​[21−12/(20⋅19)]=174.7368421053.

Standard deviation

σU=σU2=174.7368421053=13.21880638.\sigma_U=\sqrt{\sigma_U^2}=\sqrt{174.7368421053}=13.21880638.σU​=σU2​​=174.7368421053​=13.21880638.

This is the null standard deviation of U, also often called the standard error of the test statistic. It is neither the variance 174.7368 nor the standard error of a mean strength.

Standardize the directional U

Z=U−μUσU.Z=\frac{U-\mu_U}{\sigma_U}.Z=σU​U−μU​​.

With R's standard-first U=30.5 and a lower-tail alternative, the continuity-corrected value is Zcc=(30.5−50+0.5)/13.21880638=−1.437346115Z_{cc}=(30.5-50+0.5)/13.21880638=-1.437346115Zcc​=(30.5−50+0.5)/13.21880638=−1.437346115. Without correction the numerator would be −19.5. In the lecture's complementary convention, U=69.5 produces the opposite sign and an upper tail.

Read the normal tail and decide

pless=Φ(Zcc)=Φ(−1.437346115)=0.0753098358.p_{less}=\Phi(Z_{cc})=\Phi(-1.437346115)=0.0753098358.pless​=Φ(Zcc​)=Φ(−1.437346115)=0.0753098358.

At α=.05, this exceeds the threshold and fails to reject. For a two-sided alternative use 2Φ(−∣Zcc∣)2\Phi(-|Z_{cc}|)2Φ(−∣Zcc​∣), approximately .15062. Using the smaller U and then a single tail would incorrectly halve a two-sided p-value.

Worked example: chemically treated kraft paper

  1. Original question and data

    Do chemically treated pieces tend to be stronger than standard pieces? Each column contains ten independently sampled paper pieces; rows are presentation positions, not matched pairs.

  2. State design and hypotheses

    Use independent samples. Under a common-shape location model, H0:θstandard=θtreatedH_0:\theta_{standard}=\theta_{treated}H0​:θstandard​=θtreated​ and Ha:θstandard<θtreatedH_a:\theta_{standard}<\theta_{treated}Ha​:θstandard​<θtreated​. Choose α=.05 before calculation.

  3. Pool observations and handle ties

    The two 1.29 values occupy positions 3 and 4, giving 3.5 each. The two 1.37 values occupy positions 7 and 8, giving 7.5 each. Ties are pooled even when both observations come from the same group.

  4. Show both rank sums

    Standard: 2+12+6+17+9+1+14+11+3.5+10=85.52+12+6+17+9+1+14+11+3.5+10=85.52+12+6+17+9+1+14+11+3.5+10=85.5. Treated: 15+7.5+20+16+5+3.5+18+7.5+13+19=124.515+7.5+20+16+5+3.5+18+7.5+13+19=124.515+7.5+20+16+5+3.5+18+7.5+13+19=124.5. Total 210=20(21)/2210=20(21)/2210=20(21)/2.

  6. Select an appropriate reference distribution

    The ordinary integer no-tie table cannot accept U=30.5 as an exact tied statistic. Conditional permutation of the twenty observed ranks gives 184756 label allocations and 13706 lower-tail allocations, so exact one-sided p=13706/184756=0.0741843296p=13706/184756=0.0741843296p=13706/184756=0.0741843296. The separately identified tie-corrected normal method gives p=.0753098358.

  7. Decision and context

    Both p-values exceed .05. Fail to reject equal location at 5%; the observed tendency toward stronger treated paper is insufficient at this level. Under a prespecified 10% one-sided level these data would reject. That change reflects a different decision threshold, not different arithmetic.

Self-check: why are U=14 and R W=2 both correct?

In the page-24 example, 14 cross pairs have X<Y and two have X>Y. The lecture counts the first direction; R's adjusted first-sample rank sum counts the second. They are complementary and lead to the same two-sided evidence.

The independent-sample use of wilcox.test

Use the stats function with paired=FALSE, its default. Its printed W is the first group's raw rank sum minus its smallest possible rank sum. That is the U_R defined in Mathematics, complementary to the lecture's U_L.

wilcox.test(x, y, paired = FALSE, mu = 0,
            alternative = "two.sided", exact = NULL,
            correct = TRUE, conf.int = FALSE)
  • x,y: independent numeric samples; their lengths may differ. Omit missing observations independently in each sample.
  • paired=FALSE: compare independent groups. TRUE would subtract aligned rows and answer a different question.
  • mu: hypothesized shift between distributions, normally 0.
  • alternative="less": x is shifted lower than y; "greater" reverses direction; "two.sided" uses both directions.
  • exact: use the exact no-tie distribution for suitable small samples or request the normal approximation with FALSE. The lecture's R 4.5 defaults use an approximation for ties.
  • correct: a continuity correction for the normal approximation. It does not change an exact p-value.
  • conf.int=TRUE: request a location interval. Its estimated shift is based on pairwise differences; in general it is not simply median(x)−median(y).

Lecture page 29: unequal lengths and missing values

x <- c(78, 80, 67, 91, 86, 56, 96)
y <- c(85, 95, 70, 84, 79, NA, NA)
y.finite <- y[is.finite(y)]
r <- rank(c(x, y.finite))
raw.rank.sum <- sum(r[seq_along(x)])
W <- raw.rank.sum - length(x) * (length(x) + 1) / 2
c(n.x = length(x), n.y = length(y.finite), raw.rank.sum, W = W)
wilcox.test(x, y, paired = FALSE, alternative = "two.sided",
            exact = TRUE)
# First-sample raw rank sum = 44; W = 44 - 28 = 16
# Effective sample sizes: 7 and 5
Wilcoxon rank sum exact test
W = 16, p-value = 0.8763
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

The two NA entries pad a printed column; they do not remove the sixth and seventh x values because the groups are independent. The exact p-value is .8762626263, so fail to reject at .05. The lecture's complementary U would be 7(5)−16=197(5)-16=197(5)−16=19, not the printed W=16.

Reproduce page 24 by counting and ranks

x <- c(11, 15, 19, 25)
y <- c(21, 24, 28, 29)
U.lecture <- sum(outer(x, y, "<")) + 0.5 * sum(outer(x, y, "=="))
r <- rank(c(x, y))
W.raw <- sum(r[seq_along(x)])
W.R <- W.raw - length(x) * (length(x) + 1) / 2
c(U.lecture = U.lecture, W.raw = W.raw, W.R = W.R)
wilcox.test(x, y, paired = FALSE, exact = TRUE)
U.lecture W.raw W.R
       14    12   2
Wilcoxon rank sum exact test
W = 2, p-value = 0.1143

outer() compares every x with every y; its matrix has n₁ rows and n₂ columns. sum() counts TRUE comparisons. rank(c(x,y)) assigns pooled ranks. The exact CDF for a no-tie statistic is available as pwilcox(q,m,n), for example 2*pwilcox(2,4,4) gives .1142857143.

Complete runnable kraft-paper analysis

standard <- c(1.21, 1.43, 1.35, 1.51, 1.39, 1.17, 1.48, 1.42, 1.29, 1.40)
treated <- c(1.49, 1.37, 1.67, 1.50, 1.31, 1.29, 1.52, 1.37, 1.44, 1.53)
pooled.ranks <- rank(c(standard, treated))
data.frame(standard, standard.rank = pooled.ranks[1:10],
           treated, treated.rank = pooled.ranks[11:20])
sum(pooled.ranks[1:10])
# 85.5
wilcox.test(standard, treated, paired = FALSE,
            alternative = "less", exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
# Independently computed extension of the lecture's raw-data exercise
Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
W = 30.5, p-value = 0.07531
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is less than 0

The first group is standard paper, so less asks whether standard is lower than treated. W=30.5 equals 85.5−55. Reversing sample order and using greater answers the same scientific question. At .05 fail to reject.

Optional exact tied-rank enumeration

# Teaching calculation for N=20 only: choose which 10 ranks are standard.
r <- rank(c(standard, treated))
possible.W <- combn(seq_along(r), 10,
                    FUN = function(i) sum(r[i]) - 55)
observed.W <- sum(r[1:10]) - 55
c(extreme = sum(possible.W <= observed.W),
  allocations = length(possible.W),
  p.value = mean(possible.W <= observed.W))
extreme      allocations       p.value
13706        184756            0.07418433

Repeated observed rank values remain distinct observational positions when group labels are permuted; combn() counts those positions. Do not force an ordinary no-tie exact algorithm to treat half-integer W as an integer statistic. The exact tied result and the approximation are close here, but they are labeled separately.

Copyable exam example

fit <- wilcox.test(standard, treated, paired = FALSE,
                   alternative = "less", exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
fit$statistic
fit$p.value

The independent rank-sum test gives W=30.5 and a tie-corrected normal one-sided p-value of .07531. At 5% the evidence is insufficient to conclude that treated paper has a higher location, under a common-shape location interpretation. The lecture's U is the complementary 69.5.

Kruskal–Wallis Test

Rank several independent groups together, measure rank separation, and connect H to the chi-square distribution.

Lecture 4, slides 33–41

A rank comparison for several independent groups

One-way ANOVA compares group means using quantitative deviations. Kruskal–Wallis uses pooled ranks to ask whether several independent population distributions are the same. Imagine a quality engineer sampling defects from three separate assembly lines. An unusually high average rank for one line suggests its defect counts tend higher.

Let k denote the number of groups, nin_ini​ the sample size in group i, and N=∑iniN=\sum_i n_iN=∑i​ni​ the total sample size. Unequal group sizes are permitted. Under the lecture's common-shape location model, test H0:θ1=⋯=θkH_0:\theta_1=\cdots=\theta_kH0​:θ1​=⋯=θk​ against the alternative that at least two locations differ. More generally the null is equality of distributions; a rejection does not by itself identify a pair, a cause, or a median shift when shapes differ.

The samples and their observations must be independently selected. Do not use this test for repeated measurements from the same people across k conditions. The chi-square reference is an approximation; the lecture considers it adequate when every group has at least five observations. An exact or permutation method is preferable for genuinely small groups when available.

Rank everything together before calculating

Group rank sums and average ranks

Ri=∑j=1nirij,Rˉi=Rini.R_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}r_{ij},\qquad\bar R_i=\frac{R_i}{n_i}.Ri​=j=1∑ni​​rij​,Rˉi​=ni​Ri​​.

rijr_{ij}rij​ is the pooled rank of observation j in group i. Rank within the entire N-observation collection, not separately within each group. Assembly-line substitution: R1=120R_1=120R1​=120 and n1=10n_1=10n1​=10, so Rˉ1=120/10=12\bar R_1=120/10=12Rˉ1​=120/10=12. This average rank describes that line's position relative to all three lines.

The overall expected rank

Rˉ=1+2+⋯+NN=N(N+1)/2N=N+12.\bar R=\frac{1+2+\cdots+N}{N}=\frac{N(N+1)/2}{N}=\frac{N+1}{2}.Rˉ=N1+2+⋯+N​=NN(N+1)/2​=2N+1​.

For N=30, the rank total is 30(31)/2=46530(31)/2=46530(31)/2=465 and the overall average is 465/30=15.5465/30=15.5465/30=15.5. Midranks preserve this total even when observations tie. Under equal distributions, each group's average rank should fluctuate around 15.5.

Rank-based between-group variation

V=∑i=1kni(Rˉi−Rˉ)2.V=\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i(\bar R_i-\bar R)^2.V=i=1∑k​ni​(Rˉi​−Rˉ)2.

V is the lecture's rank analogue of ANOVA's between-group sum of squares. It is not itself the variance of all ranks. Assembly substitution: 10(12−15.5)2+10(21.05−15.5)2+10(13.45−15.5)210(12-15.5)^2+10(21.05-15.5)^2+10(13.45-15.5)^210(12−15.5)2+10(21.05−15.5)2+10(13.45−15.5)2. The three terms are 122.5, 308.025, and 42.025, giving V=472.55V=472.55V=472.55. Larger V means greater group separation in average rank.

Scale variation into H

H=12VN(N+1).H=\frac{12V}{N(N+1)}.H=N(N+1)12V​.

Without a tie correction, H=12(472.55)/(30⋅31)=6.0974193548H=12(472.55)/(30\cdot31)=6.0974193548H=12(472.55)/(30⋅31)=6.0974193548. Scaling makes H comparable with a chi-square reference as sample sizes grow. H is nonnegative; evidence comes from large values in its upper tail.

The equivalent rank-sum formula

H=12N(N+1)∑i=1kRi2ni−3(N+1).H=\frac{12}{N(N+1)}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{R_i^2}{n_i}-3(N+1).H=N(N+1)12​i=1∑k​ni​Ri2​​−3(N+1).

Assembly substitution: 12930[1202/10+210.52/10+134.52/10]−93\frac{12}{930}[120^2/10+210.5^2/10+134.5^2/10]-9393012​[1202/10+210.52/10+134.52/10]−93. The bracket is 1440+4431.025+1808.025=7679.051440+4431.025+1808.025=7679.051440+4431.025+1808.025=7679.05. This gives the same H=6.0974193548. The formula is convenient when group rank sums have already been calculated.

Ties and the number R actually reports

Tie correction factor

C=1−∑j(tj3−tj)N3−N,Hcorrected=HC.C=1-\frac{\sum_j(t_j^3-t_j)}{N^3-N},\qquad H_{corrected}=\frac{H}{C}.C=1−N3−N∑j​(tj3​−tj​)​,Hcorrected​=CH​.

tjt_jtj​ is a tied group's size in the complete pooled sample. For the assembly data, two observations equal 13, so C=1−(23−2)/(303−30)=0.9997775306C=1-(2^3-2)/(30^3-30)=0.9997775306C=1−(23−2)/(303−30)=0.9997775306. Thus Hcorrected=6.0974193548/0.9997775306=6.0987761460H_{corrected}=6.0974193548/0.9997775306=6.0987761460Hcorrected​=6.0974193548/0.9997775306=6.0987761460. With no ties C=1; with all observations identical C=0 and a meaningful rank-separation test is unavailable.

Degrees of freedom and the rejection boundary

df=k−1,reject if Hcorrected>χ1−α,k−12.df=k-1,\qquad\text{reject if }H_{corrected}>\chi^2_{1-\alpha,k-1}.df=k−1,reject if Hcorrected​>χ1−α,k−12​.

There are k group averages with one overall-rank constraint. For k=3, df=2. At α=.05 the upper 5% boundary is χ.95,22=5.991464547\chi^2_{.95,2}=5.991464547χ.95,22​=5.991464547. The statistic 6.098776 exceeds it, so reject.

The approximate upper-tail p-value

p=P(χk−12≥Hcorrected).p=P(\chi^2_{k-1}\ge H_{corrected}).p=P(χk−12​≥Hcorrected​).

With df=2 and H=6.098776146, p=0.0473879135p=0.0473879135p=0.0473879135. In this special df=2 case the survival probability is e−H/2e^{-H/2}e−H/2. The uncorrected lecture H=6.097419 gives p=.04742007; substituting the lecture's rounded H=6.097 gives its displayed .04743002. These small differences have identifiable rounding and tie-correction causes.

Source discrepancy, slide39. The displayed substitution prints 210², although slide38 correctly lists R₂=210.5. H≈6.097 requires 210.5²; inserting210² would give H≈5.826129. Worked example: advertising campaigns

Fifteen market areas were randomly assigned, five per campaign. In each area 400 adults were sampled and the proportion recognizing the product was recorded. The statistical units for this analysis are the 15 areas, not 6000 independent area-level observations.

Campaign1RankCampaign2RankCampaign3Rank
.3311.5.286.211.5
